en: Now begins the first quarter (pāda) of the fourth chapter.
Once the relationship between the subordinate (śeṣa) and the principal (śeṣin) has been established, what is the prompted (prayojya) and what is the prompter (prayojaka)?
Thus, because [the fourth chapter] arises in dependence [on the third], he speaks this for the purpose of refuting that [objection].
By this, the sequential relationship between the third and fourth chapters has been established.
(First Section on Propositions—Sūtra:
Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into that which subserves the sacrifice and that which subserves the person. Jaimini 4.1.1.
In the first section of the first quarter of the fourth chapter, he formulates the following point:
"Should reflection not be performed, or should it be performed, regarding that which serves the purpose of the sacrifice and that which serves the purpose of man?
It should not be performed because it lacks a fruit; [one might argue] let this [reflection] be employed for the sake of application. (MJaiNy 4.1.2)
In some cases, this [application] is stated through deliberation; in some, by virtue of the injunction of the fruit;
and in some, it is stated directly—thus, in this chapter, its application is described in many ways.
[This is] for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).
If it is argued: "We see no purpose whatsoever for this discrimination, thinking 'this is the goal of human endeavor';
therefore, like an inquiry into a crow's teeth, this inquiry should be disregarded"—do not say so.
Because the application [of a rule] can be understood through that investigation;
therefore, everything useful for determining the application—whether directly or indirectly—must be considered here.
(Regarding the second section, which defines the characteristics of that which is for the sake of the sacrifice and that which is for the sake of the person—the Sūtra:
"That in which there is pleasure for the person, there is a desire for it because it is characterized by a purpose, as it is not [otherwise] divided. Jaimini 4.1.2.

If it is said that "that which is to be performed within a ritual is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*)," there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the *godohana* vessel and others.

If it is said that "that which is desired by the person is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)," there is over-extension to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, because they too are desired by the person due to their being things to be performed.
Therefore, if it is argued that the unseen definitions of these two are difficult to determine:
Not so;
that which is enjoined solely for the sake of the excellence of the ritual's own nature is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*).
The *prayāja* offerings and others are of such a kind.
For no particular pleasure arises in the person by means of the *prayāja* and other such rites,
by which they would become ends for the person (*puruṣārtha*).
Rather, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice attains through those *prayāja* and other rites a state of perfection characterized by the capacity to produce the fruit.
Therefore, those [acts] are for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). That which is enjoined for the pleasure of the person is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*);
such are the New and Full Moon sacrifices and so forth, as well as the *godohana* vessel and so forth.
For the excellence of no sacrifice whatsoever arises from the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, because these two alone constitute the sacrifice;
nor is the godohana vessel for the sake of the sacrifice.
Even in the absence of that [Soma], the perfection of the sacrifice is accomplished by means of the cup (camasa).
Therefore, the definition of both of those [the Soma and the cup] is well-established.

In the second section of the fourth chapter, verse 1.5, [the author] formulates the argument: "Is the fruit that which is to be enjoined, or not? If the former, then it is like other [factors], because it is a constituent part of the productive operation (bhāvanā)."
The portion to be cultivated (the result) cannot be that which is enjoined, because one engages in it out of passion (*rāga*).
In the case of the injunction, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," heaven is heard as the fruit. In this regard—the disputed fruit is not what is to be enjoined—because...
If it is argued that this is because [the action] is a constituent part of cultivation (bhāvanā), like the instrument (karaṇa) and like the procedure (itikartavyatā).
Not so;
for an injunction (vidhāna) is that which impels one toward what has not yet been undertaken.

As for the fruit, however, a person is already spontaneously impelled by passion (*rāga*) due to its inherent attractiveness; thus, an injunction regarding it would be purposeless. (Mīmāṃsājñānakāṇḍa 4.1.5)
Now he formulates the third section of the *Mīmāṃsājātinī*: "The *godohana* vessel serves two purposes, or does it not? Its dual purpose is established because of its manifestation."
The accomplishment of the sacrifice can be achieved otherwise as well; that [use of the *godohana*] is solely for the sake of the person.

Regarding the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One should fetch water with a wooden cup (*camasa*); [one should fetch water] with a *godohana* [vessel] for one who desires cattle.
In this regard, there is both the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) and the status of being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatva*) concerning the *godohana*.

If it is argued that there are these two aspects— namely, that human satisfaction appears through the production of the fruit for the animal, and the perfection of the sacrifice also appears through the carrying forward of the water—
this is not so.
Let it be that the result is not accomplished without the *godohana* vessel, and thus it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*);
however, since the sacrifice (*kratu*) is accomplished even in its absence by means of a *camasa* cup, it does not serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).
In the fourth section, he formulates [the inquiry]:
"The description of substances would be for the sake of the sacrifice or for the sake of the person; this [occurs] within the sacrifice."
Because it is mandatory, its status as a human goal is evident; its being for the sake of the sacrifice is merely implied.

For a Brāhmaṇa, the acquisition of wealth through receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and teaching are the only prescribed means, as they are heard of in various scriptural passages; for a Rājanya, [the means] such as conquest and so forth are prescribed.
For the Vaiśya, it consists of agriculture and so forth;
for the Śūdra, it consists of service and so forth. And this acquisition of wealth is for the sake of the sacrifice.
Why?
Because the means of acquisition are restricted;
however, since human pleasure is accomplished by any substance whatsoever, the restriction on the means of acquisition is useless in that regard.
Regarding the sacrifice, since the *niyamāpūrva* (the unseen merit of restriction) is connected to the *paramāpūrva* (the ultimate unseen merit), the restriction (*niyama*) serves a purpose;
such being the position reached, we reply: in the acquisition of wealth, passion (*rāga*) is observed to be the motivator, so no injunction (*vidhi*) is required;
furthermore, the result, consisting of the cessation of hunger and so forth, is indeed perceived.
For this very reason, it is recorded in the Smṛti:
"Of his six duties, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of pure gifts."
If, however, it were for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*), the sacrifice itself could not be accomplished due to the absence of life.

But if it is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatā*), then—just like eating and other acts that produce pleasure in this world—the sacrifice produces pleasure in the hereafter; thus, because it is included within the goals of the person, its being for the sake of the sacrifice is established as a matter of course.
Furthermore, the restriction regarding the means is justified by the intention to indicate that there is sin (*pratyavāya*) in using alternative means.
Therefore, the acquisition of wealth is for the sake of human purpose.

(Third Section: On the fact that the Prajāpati-vows have man as their purpose; Sūtras 3–6) Upon the abandonment of that [substance], the ritual acts are for the sake of the person, because the scripture is not subject to doubt; nor is a substance intended to be processed, since there is a connection with that purpose, and thus the scriptural mention of the person pertains to the action. (Jaimini 4.1.3) But because the scripture makes no distinction, the results should follow according to the scriptural statement. (Jaimini 4.1.4)

Or rather, [the Veda is not authoritative] because, when its cause is not apprehended, there is no connection with the object for that purpose; and likewise in the case of worldly things. Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.5–6.

The third section formulates the following: "One should not look at the rising sun"—is this for the sake of the sacrifice or not? The first [view] holds it is not; because no fruit [for the person] can be postulated, what is established in the context of the sacrifice is here prohibited. (MJaiNy 4.1.8)

By the statement of a vow (*vrata*), there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*); here, that [exclusion] is a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding non-looking. It is not for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), because it is not equal to a constituent part of the sacrifice; rather, it is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), for the destruction of sin.
Without reference to any specific rite, it is heard in scripture: "One should never look at the rising sun, nor at the setting sun."
In this context, the word "nañ" expresses a prohibition (pratiṣedha) through its primary denotative function (abhidhāvṛtti), and not an exclusion by implication (paryudāsa).
Furthermore, a prohibition is necessarily preceded by a prior possibility of occurrence.
Furthermore, the Vedic prohibition of what is Vedic is closely proximate;
such being the case, wherever looking at the sun is enjoined as part of a ritual sacrifice, this prohibition applies with reference to the times of sunrise and sunset.

This being the case, a fruit need not be postulated. If one were to accept that [the prohibition] has human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) by relying on a relative negation (*paryudāsa*), then a fruit would have to be postulated for the sake of establishing the qualification (*adhikāra*). Therefore, since it is established that the prohibition is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*)—this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)— [The siddhāntin replies: No, because it is a prohibition. For when there is a prohibition, a fruit must necessarily be postulated. Otherwise, the person would engage in the prohibited act even at the cost of their own ruin. Furthermore, since the prohibition is connected with the Veda, it cannot be understood as having no fruit. And because it is a prohibition, it does not have the character of a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice; rather, its purpose is the avoidance of sin. Moreover, the qualification for the performance of the sacrifice is established by the mere knowledge of the prohibition, and thus a fruit does not need to be postulated. Therefore, the prohibition is indeed for the sake of the sacrifice. However, this is not so; rather, it is for the sake of the person, because it is a prohibition. Furthermore, since it is connected with the Veda, it cannot be understood as being without fruit. And because it is a prohibition, it lacks the character of a constituent part of the sacrifice; rather, its purpose is the avoidance of sin. Moreover, the qualification for the performance of the sacrifice is established by the mere knowledge of the prohibition, and thus a fruit need not be postulated. Therefore, the prohibition is for the sake of the person. This is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). We reply: Since it is recited following the introductory statement "His vow," namely, "He shall not look at the rising sun," something in the form of non-looking must be performed.
And that is possible only if [the negative particle] functions as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion).
In the case of a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), the meaning of the negative particle would be the mere absence of looking.
In the view of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), however, the term "not" (*nañ*) indicates by implication (*lakṣaṇā*) a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) other than looking and so forth;
and that resolve is enjoined here as a vow (*vrata*) to be performed.
Although there exist many activities other than looking and so forth that are fit for performance, [it is this specific resolve that is intended].
Nevertheless, since no specific bodily or vocal activity is perceived, and because mental activity is unavoidable, intention (*saṃkalpa*) alone remains as the [prohibited] act.
And the object to be intended, by virtue of proximity, is the negation of the root-meaning.
That being the case, the resolve in the form, "I shall not look at the sun as it rises or as it sets," is enjoined here as something to be performed;
yet that resolve does not constitute an auxiliary element (*aṅga*) of a sacrificial rite (*kratu*).

Because there is an absence of authoritative means of knowledge, such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) or indicative mark (*liṅga*), to establish that [the non-seeing is for the sake of the ritual].
Nor is there an absence of authority even if it were for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*);

for by the sentence, "By this much one becomes free from sin," the text introduces the connection of the person who beholds with demerit (*pratyavāya*), and then establishes the resolve not to look, which has the result of warding off that demerit.
Because it is understood from the injunction that these have the person as their purpose;
for if there were an intention to make them auxiliary to the sacrifice, then a counter-argument consisting of the deficiency of the sacrifice would have been presented.
Therefore, the Prajāpati-vows, such as the resolve not to look [at the rising sun], serve the purpose of the person.
(Regarding the section on the restatement of sacrificial implements in the fourth [pāda], sūtras 7–10:

"But the substances, since there is no distinction [in their application], should be offered, because they would otherwise be purposeless. (Jaimini 4.1.7) "However, the substances are connected with their own respective purposes, because they serve distinct functions; therefore, they should be used according to the scriptural injunctions. (Jaimini 4.1.8)
And they are questioned during discussions on the meaning;
and because of the observation of indicative marks. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.9–10)
The fourth section formulates the following: "The ten sacrificial implements"—is this an injunction regarding their status as oblation-materials, or not?
In the first case, since they are not otherwise established, there is a combination with the *puroḍāśa* cake, or an option between them. (Jaimini Nyāya Mālā 4.1.10)
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and the like are not tenable when [a rule] is established together with its originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*).
That which is obtained from the statement "one digs with the wooden sword" (*sphyenoddhanti*) is here restated as a praise (*saṃstava*).

In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), beginning with "The wooden sword (*sphya*) and the potsherds (*kapālāni*)" and so forth, it is handed down: "These indeed are the ten sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*)."
And these are prescribed here as being the sacrificial oblations.
Why?
Because, since they are not established by other means of knowledge, they serve a purpose not previously known.
If the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) were the oblation (*havis*) in that case, then there might be either a combination (*samuccaya*) or an option (*vikalpa*) between it and these [weapons];

this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: an option or a combination with the weapons enjoined later is not possible with the sacrificial cake enjoined at the time of the original injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), namely, "the eight-pot-sherd offering for Agni" (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*).
Being "weapons" (āyudha) means being instruments of sacrifice.

This fact, established by such scriptural injunctions as "He digs with the wooden sword (sphya)" and "He cooks on the potsherds," is here restated, and the injunction regarding the gathering [of these items], namely "He gathers the sacrificial implements (yajñāyudhāni)," is thereby praised.
Therefore, there is no status as an oblation (*haviṣṭva*).
(Regarding the section on the singularity of the animal in the fifth [chapter], sūtras 11–16:
Therein, the singularity is not a constituent part of the sacrifice, because the object is subordinate;
and also because of the singular number in the scriptural statement. (Jaimini 4.1.11–12)
If it is argued that [the object] is perceived [independently], [we reply]: No;

that is not based on verbal testimony, because its authority is like that of the previous [case]. However, it is perceived as being associated with words; for when those [words] are present, that [cognition] is seen, just as the cognition of other [objects] occurs. Jaim_4.1.15.
And there is an indicative mark (liṅga) to that effect.
[Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.16] The fifth section formulates [the following]:

In the injunction "an animal is to be sacrificed," there is a question as to whether the animal's status as a subordinate element of the sacrifice exists or not when the animal is a single entity. The first view [is that it does not exist], because by virtue of the direct Vedic statement (śruti) within its own word, the animal attains the status of being subordinate to itself.

In the beginning, when one has acquired conviction for oneself, the application of the sacrifice to the animal in the ritual is appropriate as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) according to the sequence: "The sacrifice is in the rite and in the animal.
[Commentary: In the injunction "One should immolate the *agnīṣomīya* animal," the singularity of the animal is not a subordinate element of the act of sacrificing.
Because by hearing that [word], one understands its connection with the animal;
for in this very word "animal" (*paśum*), both the animal and its oneness are heard, and thus their mutual connection is understood independently of other words.
The sacrifice, however, is conveyed by another word, namely "one should immolate" (*ālabheta*).
In that case, the relationship [of the number] is understood through syntactical connection (*vākya*). Furthermore, direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful than syntactical connection.
Therefore, since oneness is not an auxiliary element of the sacrifice, the sacrifice can be performed by two or even many—this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the following is stated].
We reply: although the word "paśum" (the animal) is a single unit, nevertheless, by its stem (*prakṛti*), the animal is indicated;
by its suffix (*pratyaya*), its status as a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is indicated.
Both "oneness" and [the agent] have been specified;
therefore, the connection first occurs with the agent that is closer to oneness.
Being a *kāraka* (participant in an action) means being a cause of an action.
This being the case, the connection even with the action itself is understood by the suffix (*pratyaya*) through the medium of the *kāraka*.

Furthermore, since the specific action is supplied by another proximate word—namely, "sacrifice" (*yāga*)—the status of oneness as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the act of sacrificing is established.
And that singularity, being itself formless, is incapable of accomplishing the act of sacrifice; therefore, it subsequently delimits the substance of the animal, which is capable of doing so.
Consequently, because singularity is an auxiliary element (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, the sacrifice is not accomplished by two or three animals.

In the same way, one should understand that in such cases as "He yokes two oxen" (*anaḍvāhau yunakti*) and "In spring, he sacrifices *kapiñjala* birds," the duality and plurality are intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*).

And likewise, there is an indicative mark [to this effect]. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.17) [In the sixth section concerning the intention to express the gender of the animal: Thus, the indicative mark is as follows. Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.17.
Start MJaiNy 4,1.14.
The sixth section formulates [the following]:
"There is no intention to express the masculine gender, because such intention is of no utility;
rather, like the number, it should be intended to be expressed because it depends upon the performance [of the rite]. (MJaiNy 4.1.14)
In the injunction "one should sacrifice an animal" (*paśumālabheta*), the masculine gender in the word *paśu* is not intended to be significant.
Why?
Because its utility is not observed either in the investigation of the meaning of the word or in the investigation of the ritual performance.
Even though the referent "tree" lacks gender, the masculine word *vṛkṣa* is employed;
likewise, even with reference to a male individual, the feminine word *makṣikā* is employed.
Therefore, there is no intention to express gender as the meaning of a word.
The performance [of the rite] is also the same for both a male individual and a female individual,
because there is no difference in the state of being an animal (paśutva) as delimited by oneness.
Therefore, since it is concluded that "gender is not intended to be significant" (avivakṣitaṃ liṅga),—
We reply: Just as the universal "cowness" (paśutva-jāti), or just as that numerical oneness (ekatva)—
the meaning of a word is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) in the linguistic usage of elders, which are not otherwise accounted for.
Likewise, why should the gender marker (*liṅga*) not also have the status of being a word-meaning?

As for the words *vṛkṣa* and *makṣikā*, we do not assert their correctness based on their actual meaning; rather, their correctness is established solely by the force of usage by those who are learned (*abhiyukta*).
Nor is there equality in the performance [of the rite],
because there is a specific distinction regarding the male and female organs;

for while the nourishment of various limbs is heard of at the time of their nourishment through mantras such as "May your speech swell," there is the hearing of the nourishment of that specific limb [the penis] through the mantra, "May the penis swell."
Therefore, just like singularity, the masculine gender is also intended to be significant.

(Seventh [Adhikaraṇa]: On the fact that those things which depend [on another] have an unseen purpose; Sūtras 18–20) In the case of dependent [rites], the existence [of the action] should be understood as having a purpose without distinction. (Jaimini 4.1.18) But in the case of an injunction, there is no commencement [of a separate rite], because it is distinct; for it is not enjoined by another. (Jaimini 4.1.19)

Or rather, when there is a desire to perform a substance, there may be a loss of its quality because it becomes subordinate to the purpose of the action. (Jaimini 4.1.20). He formulates the seventh section as follows:
The *sviṣṭakṛt* [offering] is exhausted when it has performed its function of consecration; furthermore, it is also useful for the transcendental result (*apūrva*).
Since it is logical that there be a single purpose within one ritual action, it follows that [the substance] is exhausted therein.
The consecration of the deity occurs through the mantra; the consecration of the substance occurs through its offering.
Through the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*), a new transcendental potency (*apūrva*) arises, and that [potency] is subsumed under the primary *apūrva*.
Regarding this sacrifice to Sviṣṭakṛt: there is no dispute that it is a consecration of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) that has already been employed.

In this regard, since the *saṃskāra* (consecration) necessarily exists because its visible purpose (*dṛṣṭaprayojana*) is established, the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice is exhausted by that alone and does not contribute toward an unseen potency (*apūrva*).

For it is not logical for there to be two purposes in a single ritual action—this being the position reached, we reply: even though the action is one, a difference in purpose is not contradictory due to the distinction between its constituent parts (*aṃśabheda*).
The recitation of the mantra,
the casting of the substance,
and the renunciation (tyāga) with reference to the deity.
Thus there are three parts.
Among them, through the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*), an intermediate transcendental result (*avāntarāpūrva*) is produced, which serves the supreme transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*).
Therefore, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering serves both purposes.
In this same way, the final fore-offering (antyaprayāja) and the animal-cake offering (paśupuroḍāśa) are also to be carried forth [as separate offerings].

(Regarding the eighth section, which is the formal proposition concerning the consideration of application: "Because of the equality or inequality of the purpose, [there is a distinction] among substances and actions. — Jaimini 4.1.21.

He formulates the eighth section: "Is the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) to be considered in the subsequent text, or something else? It is not the subordinate, because it is not established here by the means of knowledge (*māna*), nor by the result called application (*prayukti*). [Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāyamālā-vistara 4.1.17]
In the topics to be discussed hereafter, the very question of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) is the object of inquiry;
for example, as in the topics already passed, [the question was]: "Is this subsidiary to the sacrifice (*kratu*), or is it subsidiary to the person (*puruṣa*)?"
If it is argued that this was thought in that manner,
and why?
Because, as will be seen from the subsequent text, there appears in various places a discussion regarding the subsidiary status (*śeṣatva*) of the leaves and other items.
Not so;

for it is the result of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*), which consists in being prompted [to act], that is primarily investigated. Subsidiarity itself, however, exists by virtue of its utility toward that [result]; therefore, the investigation of subsidiarity is not the primary subject.

(Ninth Section: On the Subservience to Āmikṣā; [The Vājina Principle], Sūtras 22–24) Sūtra 22: Because they are accomplished by a single act, everything should be equal. Sūtra 23: Or rather, the *āmikṣā* would be the primary element, because it is produced through the combination of substances and the extraction of flavor.
"And because of the designation by the primary term. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.24).
He formulates the ninth section as follows:
Should both the *āmikṣā* and the *vājina* be the motivators for bringing the curd, since the capacity of both is equal? Or rather, is it the *āmikṣā* alone? Therefore, we hold the latter view.

In this case, it is the milk that is the primary factor, because of its connection with the word "payas" (milk) in the mantra and its essential nature; the whey (*vājina*) is merely a byproduct arising subsequently.
Thus it is recited: "One pours curds into hot milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas, and the whey is for the Vājins."

In this regard, just as the substance *āmikṣā* is produced by the addition of curd to milk, so too is the substance *vājina* produced; thus, the capacity of bringing in the curd to act as a generator is equal with respect to both substances.
Therefore, when it is argued that both are equally the motivators (*prayojaka*), [the following is stated]:
We reply: it is understood from words such as "that" (*tat*) and others that curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) is not a different substance, but rather milk itself;
[it is that] milk into which curds have been poured.
The word "āmikṣā" refers to milk by means of the pronoun "tat.
Thus it is recited in the *puronuvākyā* of the *āmikṣā* sacrifice: "May they enjoy the appropriate milk.
And the sweet essence of milk persists in the *āmikṣā*.
But not so for the whey (*vājina*). Therefore, since curds are brought in primarily to produce the state of curdling in the milk, the *āmikṣā* alone is the motivator; the whey is merely a byproduct.
But it is not the instigator.
(Regarding the tenth section [of the fourth book], the topic concerning the fact that the bringing of the cows is not prompted by the act of placing the foot-steps—sūtra:
"The act of placing the foot-steps does not prompt the bringing, because it is for the sake of another.
Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.25.
The tenth section formulates the following:
In the bringing of the *somakrayaṇī* cow, is the ritual action regarding her footprint the motivator?
Or not? The first [position] holds that it is, because the anointing of the axle, like the purchase itself, is in close proximity [to the footprint]. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 4.1.20)
By the third [reason], the cow is for the purpose of purchase, and the act of bringing it is for that purpose through the medium of the cow;
therefore, it is prompted by that [purchase], and thus there is no prompting power in the word [‘ekahāyanī’] itself.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the purchase of Soma is enjoined: "He purchases [Soma] with a one-year-old cow (ekahāyanī)."
When a one-year-old tawny cow is brought to purchase the Soma, the Adhvaryu follows behind her;
this is also recorded in the scripture: "He steps out after her for six steps."
Then, having placed gold upon the seventh step and offered an oblation, one should take up the dust that has settled on that step.
Regarding this, it is also heard in scripture: "The Adhvaryu takes up the seventh step with his joined palms.
Having collected that dust, one should place it—mixed with collyrium—upon the axle of the two *havirdhāna* carts.

This too has been heard: having introduced the topic with "They indeed prepare the sacrifice when they [take] the footprint of the Soma-purchase cow," it continues, "When they move the two Havirdhāna carts forward, then one should smear the axle with that [clay].
In that case, as the purchase is proximate, [the clay from the footprint is connected to the axle-smearing].
In the same way, the act of placing the foot and the application of collyrium to the eyes are proximate [to their respective purposes].
Now, it might be argued that just as the bringing of curds is connected with the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture), [so too is the action connected with its specific result].
"It is not the case that the application of collyrium to the eyes is connected with the bringing forward of the Soma-purchasing cow"—
this is not correct; for the lack of connection with the purchase itself is equally applicable.

Now, if it is argued that even though the purchase is not directly connected with the bringing of the cow, it is nonetheless accomplished by it— and therefore the application of collyrium to the dice is likewise accomplished by it because the principle is the same— then it follows that, just like the purchase itself,
the ritual action of the word [the mantra] is also the motivator for the bringing of the Soma-purchasing cow. This being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):

We reply: By the direct scriptural statement (śruti) of the instrumental case in "He buys with a one-year-old cow," it is understood that the cow is for the purpose of the purchase. Since the bringing [of the cow] is also for the sake of the purchase through the medium of the cow, the purchase itself is the motivator for the bringing.
Furthermore, neither the cow nor its bringing is heard anywhere in scripture as being for the purpose of the foot-washing rite (padakarma).
Therefore, that is not a determining factor.
(Regarding the eleventh section, concerning the fact that the scattering of husks is not a subordinate act for the sake of the potsherds; the sūtra states:

And the action of expressing the meaning [of the mantra] is [for the sake of the future result], because of its connection with what is yet to come, since that is the cause; for it is for that purpose that it is enjoined. Jaimini 4.1.26.

He formulates the eleventh topic: "Are both baking and the pouring of husks the motivators for the use of the potsherd? Or is it only baking? [The latter], because the third case ending indicates that the pouring is for the sake of the baking."
The purpose of the *puroḍāśakapāla* (the cake-pan) would be for the sake of baking, by virtue of its name;
there is no further application of what has already been employed, nor does that entail its use in the sowing [of seeds].
— "He bakes on the potsherds" (*kapāleṣu śrapayati*); thus, the baking of the *puroḍāśa* is directly enjoined by scripture.
Likewise, in the injunction "He scatters the husks with the cake-potsherd," the potsherd's function of holding the husks is heard [in the text].
Those husks, together with the potsherd, are to be placed in the southwest direction (the region of Nirṛti) with the mantra, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases.
In that case, just as the cooking is the motivator for the preparation of the potsherd, [so too is the scattering the motivator for its use].
If it is argued that the husk-scattering is also the motivator (prayojaka),

because— just as the fact that the leading of the one-year-old cow is understood to be for the purpose of purchase from the instrumental case-ending in "ekahāyanyā"— likewise, from the instrumental case-ending in "kapālena," the fact that the potsherd is for the purpose of husk-scattering is understood.
Not so;
for here it is not merely the *kapāla* (potsherd) that is heard in scripture as the instrument for the scattering of husks (*tuṣopavāpa*).
What then? It is that *kapāla* which has been taken up and placed for the purpose of baking the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
The status of that potsherd as an instrument [of baking] is understood from its prescription by means of a name accompanied by a qualifier, namely, "with the *puroḍāśa*-potsherd.
This being the case, the potsherd is employed for the first time through the act of baking.
Furthermore, once something has been employed [for one purpose], it cannot be employed again for another by means of sowing the husks.
Therefore, the potsherd, having already been employed by the act of cooking (śrapaṇa), serves its purpose for the sowing of husks through incidental application (prasaṅga).
It is precisely this kind of subsidiary status (aṅgatva) that is understood through the direct statement of the instrumental case (tṛtīyā-śruti).

(Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.27: In the twelfth [section], concerning the fact that excrement and blood are not to be employed in the animal sacrifice— ) In the animal sacrifice, because there is no taking hold [of them], blood and excrement do not constitute ritual actions.
He formulates the twelfth topic:
"Is the heart and so forth, as well as the excrement and so forth, the motivator for the immolation of the animal?
Or rather, let it be the heart and so forth alone; for they are equal by virtue of being the subject under discussion. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nayā 4.1.24)

Because the oblation (*havis*) consists of the entirety of the substance, the heart and other parts—which are themselves of the nature of the oblation—are the motivators (*prayojaka*) for its offering; it is not so for anything else, because that does not possess such a character.
Regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīyapaśu*), it is heard in scripture: "One cuts off [the portions] first from the heart..."
"Then [he pierces] the tongue, then the chest," it is said;
likewise, another scriptural passage is heard: "He pierces completely through the excrement" and "he casts out the blood."

In this regard, if it is argued that because the heart and so forth and the dung and so forth are equally recited in the context (*prakaraṇa*) and are equally accomplished by means of the animal, the dung and so forth—just like the heart and so forth—are also the motivators (*prayojaka*) for the immolation of the animal; we say:
not so.
For the animal sacrifice is accomplished by means of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
And since the status of being an oblation (haviṣṭva) belongs only to the heart and so forth because they are fit to be consumed, and not to the unfit excrement and blood,
therefore the heart and so forth alone are the motivators (prayojaka).
The single thorough cleansing and the removal of blood—both of these are merely methods for the disposal of remnants.
(Thirteenth Section: On the Non-application of the Sviṣṭakṛt to the Puroḍāśa; Sūtras 28–32) Sūtra 28:
And that which has a single part as its substance [is used], because at the time of its origin it is connected with what is already present.
Sūtra 29: If it is argued that, on account of the specific designation, there must be another [substance] for that purpose.
Not because of the proximity of the remainder;
because of the performance of the ritual act;
and because of the observation of an indicative mark.

In the thirteenth adhikaraṇa (topic), beginning with *Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra* 4.1.26–27, he formulates the following: Is the *sviṣṭakṛt* the motivator for the two [portions], namely the northern half of the *puroḍāśa* cake?
Or rather, for the sake of establishing his own position, the first [proponent] should employ one who lives off what has been used [by others].

Since the word "uttarārdha" (the northern half) requires a correlative in the present context, let it function by depending upon the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) intended for Agni and the other deities.
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "He cuts off [a portion] for Sviṣṭakṛt from the northern half."
If it is argued that this *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice is the instigator (*prayojaka*) of some new [portion] and of its subsequent half-portion,
because in the absence of both of these, its own establishment would be impossible—
it is not so.
The words *uttara* (subsequent) and *ardha* (half), being pronominal (*sarvanāman*) and denoting a portion (*bhāga*), refer to some specific portion under discussion.
The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) intended for deities such as Agni is the portion under discussion and possesses a share.
Therefore, the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice proceeds by depending upon that very [portion].
But one is not the prompter of another.
(Chapter Fourteen: On the non-performance of retaining the remnant and its vessel at the time of the sprinkling; Sūtras 33–39) Sūtra 33:

At the sprinkling, there should be a different vessel, as in the case of the after-offerings, because of the separation [of the acts]. Sūtra 34: Or rather, not so, because it is not a separate vessel; for the lack of being a separate vessel follows from the fact that it is only a portion [of the same substance].
And because of the reason for simultaneous performance; Jaimini 4.1.35.
And because of the observation of non-existence; Jaimini 4.1.36.
When it exists, there is the mention of "with"; Jaimini 4.1.37.
If it is argued that [the result] does not belong to him, [we reply:
it would belong to him, because he is the primary [agent]. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.38–39)

He formulates the fourteenth topic: "Having performed the sprinkling (abhighāraṇa), what is done here with the remnant of the prayāja offerings? Should the holding of the remnant and its vessel be performed, or not? Or is it merely the sprinkling? [Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāyamālā-vistara 4.1.28]
Otherwise, for you, there would be neither an action nor a non-action based on performance;
and in the case of the omentum of the animal dedicated to Prajāpati, no purpose whatsoever would be served by the sprinkling [of clarified butter].
In the archetype sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "One sprinkles the sacrificial oblations with the remnant of the Prayāja offerings."
This very [procedure] is extended by analogy to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).
And the modified sacrifices in question here are the animals belonging to the Vājapeya;
these are of two kinds: the sacrificial animals (*kratupaśu*) and the animals dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatyapaśu*).

The sacrificial animals prescribed by such injunctions as "He immolates an animal dedicated to Agni" are the *kratupaśus* (animals belonging to the sacrifice). Others, however, are those prescribed by the injunction "He immolates seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati.
Both these types of animals are commenced together at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).
Consequently, for the sake of all [the animals], the *prayāja* offerings are performed only once.

Since the sacrificial animals of the *kratu* are to be immolated at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) itself, the sprinkling of their oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja* ghee is accomplished without any obstacle.
As for the animals dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatya*), their ritual performance extends only up to the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire).
The touching (ālambha), however, takes place at the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina-savana), because of the injunction regarding that specific time: "He touches [the animals] during the Brahmasāman.
Furthermore, for the purpose of sprinkling those oblations (havis) dedicated to Prajāpati and others, the remnant of the Prayāja offerings from the morning must be retained.
Furthermore, holding it in the *juhū* ladle is not possible here,
because the *juhū* is occupied during the performance of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) of the ritual (*kratu*).
Therefore, having heated another vessel, this remnant (*śeṣa*) must be held in that.
Otherwise, the accomplishment [of the rite] would follow from the sprinkling with the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings of the *prājāpatya* oblations.
Therefore, since it might be argued that "the vessel for holding the remnants and [the act of] holding it must be prepared," we reply: neither of those two need be performed.
Why?
Because pouring over (abhidhāraṇa) is a form of disposal of the remnants (śeṣapratipatti), and thus it lacks the character of a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the oblation (*havis*).
For when a visible disposal is present, an invisible refinement is not appropriate.
Moreover, the emptying of the *juhū* ladle is observed [in the ritual].

Otherwise, if the *juhū* were already filled with the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings, the [clarified butter] taken for the purpose of the *ājyabhāga* offerings would become mixed [with those remnants].
Therefore, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the sprinkling with the remnant is performed solely for the sake of the disposal (*pratipatti*) consisting of the act of emptying.
Or, even if there were also a consecration of the oblation (*havis*) therein, nevertheless, the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) over the omentum (*vapā*) dedicated to Prajāpati would be useless;
for it is sprinkled to prevent dryness,
and there is no dryness in the omentum dedicated to Prajāpati.
Because its roughness is indeed warded off by the *brahmasāman*.
For this very reason, it is heard in scripture: "The omentum is indeed as if raw when it is not yet held [by the *brahmasāman*];
the *brahmasāman* is indeed the Brahman; when one takes hold of it with the *brahmasāman*, [it becomes fit]."
"Therefore, they are held by means of a *śamyā*.
The meaning is that a *śamyā* is a wooden pin.
Consequently, the remaining acts of holding and the offering thereof should not be performed.
(Regarding the fifteenth section, concerning the fact that the act of bringing together [the butter] necessitates the properties of the *ājya* offering, Sūtras 40–41:
"But the bringing together should be primary, because of the observation of an indicative mark" (Jaimini 4.1.40).
"For when there is a direct statement, there is no need for a supporting reason" (Jaimini 4.1.41).

In the fifteenth section of the fourth chapter (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 4.1.30–32), [the author] formulates the following: "For the offering of the fourth *prayāja*, there is the clarified butter from the *aupabhṛta* vessel."
"One brings [the butter] into the *juhū*"; this [injunction] should not be applied to the *aupabhṛta* [butter].
Or rather, it should be employed because it is not illogical that it serves all purposes such as the *prayāja*s;
therefore, since there is an option between the butter in the *upabhṛt* vessel and that in the *jauhava* vessel as prescribed in the scripture.
"It is not a case of being a motivator; let it not be so. For the *jauhava* [clarified butter] has a fixed purpose.
When it is said, 'Having passed over the *iḍā*, he pours from the *aupabhṛta* into the *juhū*,' that [butter] would motivate [the action] at the fourth [pouring].
Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in the scripture: "Having passed over the *iḍā*, he pours the *aupabhṛta* [butter] into the *juhū* over the *barhis*."
The meaning of this is as follows: "Among the five *prayāja* offerings, the third *prayāja* is designated by the word *iṣ* with a plural ending.
Having passed over that third *prayāja*, one must bring into the *juhū* ladle the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) situated in the *upabhṛt* ladle in order to offer the fourth *prayāja* named *barhis*.
This bringing [of the butter] is not the motive for the taking of the clarified butter in the *upabhṛt*.

For instance, the manner of taking the clarified butter (*ājya*) and its application in the three ladles— the *juhū*, *upabhṛt*, and *dhruvā*— is thus recorded in the tradition: "One takes four [spoonfuls] in the *juhū*,
eight in the *upabhṛt*, and four in the *dhruvā*."
"That which one takes in the *juhū* ladle is for the *prayāja*s;
that which is in the *upabhṛt* is for the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s; indeed, that clarified butter (*ājya*) which is in the *dhruvā* is taken for the sake of the entire sacrifice.
In this regard, the butter in the *jauhava* [ladle] is intended solely for the *prayāja*s.
However, since the *aupabhṛta* [ladle] is for the purpose of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings, there is an option between the *jauhava* and the *aupabhṛta* regarding the *prayājas*.
This being the case, when the *prayājas* are performed with the *jauhava*, there is no bringing forward of the *aupabhṛta* at all; how, then, could there be a requirement for its bringing forward?
When the *prayāja* oblation is performed with the butter from the *aupabhṛta* ladle, then half of that *aupabhṛta* butter is for the sake of the five *prayājas*,
and the other half is for the sake of the *anuyājas*.

Since the substance intended for the *prayāja* offerings was brought into the *juhū* ladle at the very time of the first *prayāja*, no further pouring of that substance toward the fourth *prayāja* is prescribed.
However, as for the other half remaining in the *upabhṛt* for the sake of the *anuyāja*s, a certain portion of that must be poured from it toward the fourth *prayāja*.

Since [the butter] has already been employed solely for the *anuyājas*, its bringing [to the *prayājas*] is not the motive [for its use]. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: "That which belongs to the *juhū* ladle is for the purpose of the first three *prayājas*; that which belongs to the *aupabhṛt* ladle is for the purpose of the remaining two *prayājas* and for the *anuyājas*. Since such a distribution of the two sentences is possible, one should not resort to an option (*vikalpa*) that is beset by eight defects.
It is possible;
when there is the acceptance of the *jauhava* [offering], then the established authority of the sentence concerning the *aupabhṛta* [offering] would have to be abandoned.

Invalidity, which had not been accepted, would be accepted; furthermore, at some point upon the acceptance of the *aupabhṛta* [ladle], validity, which had been abandoned, would be accepted, and invalidity, which had been accepted, would be relinquished.
Thus, there are four defects in the sentence concerning the *aupabhṛta* [clarified butter],
and likewise four in the sentence concerning the *jauhava*;
thus, there are eight defects in total.
And the aforementioned arrangement is determined from the sentence "atihāyeḍaḥ" (skipping over the iḍā).
Thus, just as the after-offerings (anuyājas) are the motivators for what is contained in the upabhṛt-ladle,
so too is the bringing [of the butter] which accomplishes the fourth and fifth fore-offerings (prayāja) indeed a motivator.
(Regarding the sixteenth [adhikaraṇa], concerning the fact that the *aupabhṛta* and *jauhava* [clarified butter] serve both purposes and not both purposes respectively; Sūtras 42–45:

"In that case, the origin [of the clarified butter] would be undivided. (Jaimini 4.1.42) "In that case, the *jauhava* [butter] is for the purpose of prohibiting the *anuyāja* offerings. (Jaimini 4.1.43)
If it is argued that the same applies to the *aupabhṛta* [ladle], [we reply:
it would be so; however, because of the prohibition regarding the *juhū*, it is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*).
Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.44–45.
The sixteenth section formulates the following:
Is the clarified butter (ājya) in the *juhū*, *upabhṛt*, and *dhruvā* ladles for all purposes, or is there a fixed restriction?
It is for all purposes because there is no distinction; however, the butter in the *juhū* (*jauhava*) is indeed for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings.

The clarified butter in the *aupabhṛta* vessel would be the cause for both the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings, while the *dhruva* butter would be for the purpose of the fire-offerings; such is the settled rule considered to be established by the scriptural injunctions.

(MJaiNy 4.1.34) If it is argued that, since no specific restrictive rule is heard in the injunctions regarding the taking of butter—such as "he takes four spoonfuls in the *juhū*"—the clarified butter contained in the three vessels must therefore serve all purposes:
Not so;
for a fixed rule is understood from such sentences as, "That which he takes in the *juhū* ladle is for the *prayāja*s. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāyamālā-vistara 4.1.33–34)
(Seventeenth [topic]: On the taking of two or four portions in the *upabhṛt* ladle; Sūtras 46–48.
"That [number] is eight, because it is heard [in scripture];
and because of the favoring of the *jauhava* [clarified butter]. (Jaimini 4.1.46–47)
"But the capacity for the cause and the hearing [of the injunction] apply equally to both in the case of bringing together.
(Jaimini 4.1.48). He formulates the seventeenth adhikaraṇa as follows:

Regarding the statement "eight [ladles] in the upabhṛt," is the injunction for taking eight or one at a time, or for taking four and two? It would be the former, because the direct hearing of the number "eight" is primary.
The "four-times-taken" (*caturgṛhīta*) portion, being an integral part of the oblation, is not set aside because it possesses its own fruit;
therefore, the "fourfoldness" is indicated as being taken together for the purpose of the sacrifice.

In the sentence regarding the taking [of the offering], namely "he takes four times with the *juhū* ladle," just as a single taking of the oblation qualified by the number four is enjoined, so too [is the case here].

In the same way, regarding the statement "eight [spoonfuls] in the upabhṛt," a single act of taking an oblation qualified by the number eight must be enjoined, and not two acts of taking four spoonfuls each. This is because, such being the case, the word "eight" is understood in its primary sense. If there were an injunction of two instances of the number four—which are constituent parts of the number eight—it would result in the word "eight" being used in a figurative sense (lakṣaṇā) as a part-whole relationship. This being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):

We reply: Let the definition indeed apply [to both]. For if one were to accept the primary meaning [of the term *homa*], it would result in a contradiction with the statement regarding the oblation (*homavākya*).

The sentence heard as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), "He offers what has been taken four times" (*caturgṛhītaṃ juhoti*), prescribes the fourfold taking for the purpose of any oblation whatsoever.

Although this [rule] is general in form as it pertains to all oblations (*homa*), whereas the rule concerning the *aupabhṛta* ladle is specific in form as it pertains only to the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings,
nevertheless, because the oblation possesses a fruit and is thus primary, [the former prevails].
Since the act of drawing [the butter] is subordinate because it serves the purpose of the oblation,
it is proper to follow the primary element and use exactly four portions (caturgṛhīta), rather than eight portions (aṣṭagṛhīta) following the subordinate element.
Therefore, two sets of four portions are prescribed for the *upabhṛt* ladle.
Among these, one set of four portions is the oblation for the fourth and fifth *prayāja* offerings;
the other, however, is for the *anuyāja* offerings.

If it is argued that, in that case, since only the fourfold portion constitutes the oblation, the injunction should have been "four [spoonfuls] in the upabhṛt," and not the injunction "eight [spoonfuls] in the upabhṛt"—
this is not so.
If that were the case, the second fourfold drawing intended for the *anuyāja* offerings would not be established.

If, on the other hand, that too were enjoined by another scriptural statement, then, since the *upabhṛt* ladle would already be occupied by the first fourfold drawing, a different vessel would have to be sought for the second.
If the second *caturgṛhīta* (four-drawings) were also enjoined by the word "in the *upabhṛt*," then,
because the two *caturgṛhītas* would have to be performed separately, bringing them into the *upabhṛt* with a single effort would not be accomplished.
Therefore, the phrase "eight [drawings] in the *upabhṛt*" is stated for the purpose of bringing both together into the vicinity of that vessel.

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the coexistence [of the two], even when the word "eight" (aṣṭa) is employed, the two [portions] consisting of four ladlings each are prescribed here in order to ensure the status of the oblation (haviṣṭva).
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* by the venerable Mādhava.
Now begins the second quarter of the fourth chapter.
(In the first section, concerning the fact that the tone of voice, cutting, and so forth are not motivators [of ritual acts], there are six sūtras.)
But the *svaru* is not produced from multiple [materials], because its own word denotes its specific function; Jaimini 4.2.1.
And one might suspect it is so because of its difference in genus; Jaimini 4.2.2.
Or rather, it is a part of that [same material], because the status of being a *svaru* is caused by that [act of cutting]; Jaimini 4.2.3.
And because of the scriptural mention of "pieces" (Jaimini 4.2.4);
because it is observed [to be done] at each sacrificial post (Jaimini 4.2.5);
and because the word *karoti* is used in reference to the taking up [of the wood] (Jaimini 4.2.6).
In the second quarter (pāda), the first section (adhikaraṇa) is formulated as follows:
Regarding the injunction "make the *svaru*," the *svaru* is distinct from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Or rather, let the first [alternative] be the case, because there is an injunction of a qualified [action].

Since the specific quality called *svarutva* (the state of being a *svaru*) is enjoined for the first piece of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), it is simpler [to accept that] it is merely a by-product; therefore, it is indeed an incidental product.
In the context of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīyapaśu*), it is heard in the scripture: "He makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post."
In this regard, just as the sacrificial post (yūpa) is the motivator for the act of cutting, so too does the wooden splinter (svaru) motivate the cutting.
Why? Because by the word "makes" (karoti), a qualified injunction is understood.
For in the verbal root *karoti* (to do/make), "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) is the primary meaning;
therein, the *svādira* tree, indicated by the word "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*), is the instrument (*karaṇa*),
while cutting and so forth constitute the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
"The *svaru* is to be produced from the wood that has been cut"—this is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).
The application (*viniyoga*) of the *svaru* once it has been produced is thus recorded in scripture: "He anoints the animal with the *svaru*.
Therefore, since the *svaru* is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the cutting, this being the position reached—

We reply: "The first chip that falls from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) while it is being cut is the *svaru*. Since this merely prescribes the name "svaru," there is parsimony (*lāghava*); thus, like the sacrificial post, the *svaru* is not the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the cutting, but rather it is produced as a byproduct (*anuniṣpadyate*) of the cutting which is itself motivated by the sacrificial post.
(Regarding the second section [adhikaraṇa] on the necessity of bringing in a branch, the sūtra states:
"In the case of the branch, because it is subordinate to that [act]. Jaimini 4.2.7.
The second section formulates the argument:
In the injunction "he brings the eastern [branch]," it must be either the direction or a branch;
because of the direct mention of "direction," the direction cannot be something that is brought, and therefore it is the branch that is indicated by it.

Regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, with reference to the *palāśa* branch, it is heard in scripture: "When he drives away the calves with a *palāśa* branch," and further, "If he should bring [the branch] facing eastward, he shall conquer the world of the gods.
If it is argued that, since the word "east" (*prācī*) denotes a direction, what is being enjoined here is the bringing [of the branch] from a specific direction;
Not so; for it is impossible.
Therefore, the eastern branch of the tree is indicated here.
This being the case, there is favor toward the subject under discussion.
(Regarding the third section, on the fact that cutting is connected with the branch [Sūtras 8–9]:

Because the branch is the primary object there, the separation [of the twig] should be done with the *upaveṣa*; that would be an inconsistency. (Jaimini 4.2.8) And because of the departure from the direct scriptural statement. (Jaimini 4.2.9)
The third section (adhikaraṇa) formulates [the following]:
"Having cut a branch, one should make the *upaveṣa* from its base; with that branch..."
One should push aside the calf-skins and place the potsherds starting from the *upaveṣa*.
Two things are the motivators for cutting: either the removal of the calf, or the first [alternative].
Here, the former is [the case] because of the distribution of the application between the tip and the root.
"The statement 'He makes the *upaveṣa* from the root for another purpose' is expectant;
it is fulfilled by that which is produced as a byproduct. Therefore, it is appropriate that the *upaveṣa* be the last [action].
In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in the scripture: "Having stripped the branch from its base, he makes the *upaveṣa*."
Having cut this palāśa branch and brought it from the chest [of the tree], one should cut it again so that the root-end portion, measuring a span (prādeśa), is made into the *upaveṣa*.
Regarding those two parts—the tip and the root of the branch—a separate application is traditionally taught: "With the branch, he drives away the calves."
"One places the potsherds with the *upaveṣa*.
Thus, these two tasks are accomplished by means of the branch brought forth by the cutting of the tree.
Therefore, if it is argued that both [the *upaveṣa* and the potsherds] are equally the motivators (*prayojaka*) for the acts of cutting and bringing [the branch], then—
Not so.
When it is stated, "He makes the *upaveṣa*," there arises an expectancy as to "by what substance? and thus one must say, "from the root.
Furthermore, when the expectancy "whose root? arises again, the expectancy must be fulfilled by saying, "the root of a *palāśa* branch that has been cut for the purpose of separating the calves."
Therefore, in the act of cutting, only the driving away of the calf (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) is the efficient cause (*prayojaka*);
the fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*), however, is a by-product (*anuniṣpādī*).
But surely, let it be so for the first cutting; [what of the subsequent ones?]
If it is argued that the cutting of the second [branch] is prompted by the *upaveṣa*,
because the performance of the *upaveṣa* is enjoined by means of the root [of the branch] that has been completed by the act of peeling (*parivāsana*),
otherwise the suffix *-tva* (in the form *parivāsyopaveṣaṃ karoti*)— which expresses a common agent and anteriority in time— would be untenable.
Not so;
for the connection of the parivāsana with the upaveṣa is understood through syntactical connection (vākya),
whereas its connection with the branch is established by the direct statement (śruti) of the accusative case in the word "śākhām."
Even for a branch that has already been cut previously, a further cutting with the root as the point of departure (*apādāna*) is required;
otherwise, it would be difficult to separate the calf by lifting the branch along with its roots with one's hand.
For this very reason, the ablative case ending is heard in the word "from the root" (*mūlataḥ*), denoting the point of departure.

That being the case, just as the tree that serves as the substratum for the first cutting is worldly because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), so too is the root that serves as the substratum for the second cutting a worldly piece of wood.
Since the taking up of some piece of wood is necessarily implied when placing the potsherds upon the embers, that very act is here restated in the injunction: "He makes the *upaveṣa*."

The meaning of the statement is that when the branch has been trimmed and the root has been discarded, one should not exert effort in searching for another piece of wood for the purpose of using it as a support for the potsherds (*kapāla-upadhāna*).

This being the case, on a full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) when there is no milking, since there is no branch for the purpose of driving away the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*), the cutting of the branch for the sake of the *upaveṣa* (the fire-stirring stick) should not be performed.
(Regarding the section on the fourth [topic], that the throwing away of the branch is a disposal rite, sūtras 10–13:

"But in the case of the carrying away, it is an oblation because of the commonality of connection and because substances are subordinate to the purpose. (Jaimini 4.2.10) "Or rather, it is a disposal rite, because the word has that as its primary meaning. (Jaimini 4.2.11)
If it is argued that [the ritual] is for the sake of the purpose (*artha*), [we reply]:
No, because he has no entitlement (*anadhikāra*) to that purpose, and because the purpose has already been accomplished. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.2.12–13)
The fourth section formulates the following:

"One should cast away the *prastara* (grass-bundle) together with the branch; is this [act] a primary rite (*arthakarma*) for the sake of the branch, or is it properly understood as a secondary act of disposal (*pratipatti*)? (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 4.2.7).

The sacrifice is prescribed for the sacrificial grass (prastara); by virtue of its association with the branch, and because it is of that same nature, the act of carrying [the grass] would necessitate the branch as a subsidiary action.
The term *hṛti* (carrying away) denotes sacrifice; it cannot therefore mean a mere disposal (*pratipatti*).
Consequently, on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), the act of carrying away would not necessitate the employment of the branch.
In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in scripture: "He carries away the *prastara* [grass-bundle] together with the branch."
In that context, the striking with the branch is a preparatory act (arthakarma).
Why?
Because the word "striking" denotes the sacrifice itself.
This has been examined by taking as an example the sentence: "He throws the prastara-bundle with the sūktavāka.

If the throwing of the prastara were a sacrifice (yāga), then, by association with that, the throwing of the branch (śākhā) would also be a sacrifice, and thus it would be an *arthakarma*—that is, an action performed for a purpose, namely for the sake of the efficacy of the ritual (*kratu*).
To this, [the opponent] objects: "In that case, the *palāśa* branch should also be used in the offering on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*).
To this we reply: In the statement, "He offers the grass-bundle (*prastara*) with the *sūktavāka*," it is not stated that the verbal root *hṛ* (to offer) denotes a sacrifice (*yāga*).
Rather, having perceived a deity from the wording of the mantra itself, a sacrifice is inferred by means of both the substance and the deity.

However, in the case of the striking of the branch (*śākhā-praharaṇa*), there is no deity [to whom it could be offered]. Consequently, since it is impossible to conceive of a sacrifice (*yāga*) in that context, the verbal root *hṛ* (to take away) here denotes nothing other than the abandonment of its own primary meaning. This being the case, since the *palāśa* branch used for the removal of the calves has no further utility, and must necessarily be abandoned somewhere in order to find space at the site of the sacrifice, the scripture [prescribes] the *āhavanīya* fire as the location for that abandonment.
Thus, the relinquishment is regulated;
and by this scripturally prescribed relinquishment, there occurs the ritual processing (*pratipatti*) of the branch.
"Processing" (*pratipatti*) is a visible purpose consisting of a sanctificatory rite (*saṃskāra*).

It is just as when the king spits out his chewed betel nut into a golden spittoon; likewise, the disposal [of the offering] is an act of dedication (*pratipatti-karma*). And because by that [act], even in the absence of the [substance itself], there is no deficiency in the sacrifice (*kratuvaikalya*).
On the full moon day, one does not employ the branch that serves as the cause for its own accomplishment.

(Regarding the fifth section on the disposal of the *praṇītā* waters as a ritual act of completion, Sūtras 14–15: Because they are not connected with the original production [of the sacrifice], there should be a distribution of the *praṇītā* waters like that of the clarified butter (*ājya*).
Or rather, there is the disposal of those intended for the purpose of mixing [the flour], because the others have that as their primary purpose. (Jaimini 4.2.14–15)
The tenth and eleventh sūtras of the fourth section (adhikaraṇa) of the Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra-vṛtti formulate the fifth topic:
"He mixes with the *praṇītā* waters" and "he pours them out on the altar"— what [is the meaning of these]?
Two [uses] of water are for bringing [the grains], or else for mixing the sacrificial oblation (havis).
Since it is stated that "one carries forward the water," its purpose is twofold because of this equality;
by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), it is for the purpose of mixing [the flour], while by the act of pouring out (*ninītiḥ*), it is for the purpose of disposal (*pratipatti*).
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "One carries forward the water."

The purpose of those waters brought forth with a ladle as a vessel is heard in the scripture thus: "He mixes the sacrificial oblations with the *praṇītā* waters," and "He pours out the *praṇītā* waters within the altar."
The sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) consist of flour intended for the *puroḍāśa* cakes.
In this context, both the mixing of the offering with water and its pouring out upon the altar (*vedī*) are the purposes for which the fetching of water (*apāṃ praṇayanam*) is performed.
Why? Because...
If it is argued that this is not so because the originative injunction for the act of "driving away the waters" (*apaḥ vrajayati*) is identical in both cases,
and no specific connection with the kneading (*saṃyavana*) is perceived in this sentence—
[we reply: do not say so.

In the injunction [for the mixing], because the instrumental case-ending in the word "praṇītābhiḥ" (with the *praṇītā* waters) reveals that they are the means for the act of mixing (*saṃyavana*), the mixing itself is the motivator (*prayojaka*).

However, in the injunction for pouring out (*ninayana*), because the accusative case-ending in the word "praṇītāḥ" (the *praṇītā* waters) reveals that they are the objects to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), the pouring out is a consecration in the form of a disposal (*pratipatti*); thus, it is not the motivator for the carrying forward (*praṇayana*).
(Regarding the sixteenth through eighteenth sūtras on the topic that the giving of the staff in the sixth [chapter] is a purposeful act:

Jaimini 4.2.16) The giving of the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa is like the throwing [of the grass-bundle], because its purpose has already been fulfilled. Jaimini 4.2.17) Or rather, it is a purposeful act because of its connection with the agent, like the wearing of a garland.
"And because it is seen [to apply] even when connected with ritual action" (Jaimini 4.2.18).
He formulates the sixth section as follows:
Regarding the giving of the staff in the Maitrāvaruṇa rite, is it a disposal (*pratipatti*) or a purposeful act (*arthakarma*)?
Let the former be the case, because [the staff] has already served its purpose in being held.
The preparation of that which is to be used follows from the preparation of what has been joined and used;
[this occurs] after the standing [of the sacrificer] and the recitation of the *praisha* and *anuvacana*. The staff (*daṇḍa*) is to be expected as a subordinate element (*arthakarma*).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "When the Soma has been purchased, he gives the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa."
This giving of the staff is a rite of performance.
Why?
Because the staff has fulfilled its purpose through being held by the sacrificer.
For the sacrificer holds the staff given by the Adhvaryu for the sake of accomplishing the consecration (dīkṣā) until the purchase of the Soma;
therefore it is traditionally taught: "He consecrates with the staff," and "In that he gives the staff to the consecrated one."
If it is argued that "the giving away of a staff already employed is [an act of] practice," it is not so;
for even a future utility exists in the staff.
When the Maitrāvaruṇa priest stands and recites the *praiṣas*, at that time a staff is required for support;
for this very reason it is traditionally taught: "He recites the *praiṣas* while holding a staff."

That being the case, between a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the form of a rite of performance (*pratipatti-karma*) which has already been employed, and a consecration of the form of a rite for a purpose (*artha-karma*) which is yet to be employed, the latter is superior.
For the activity of consecration everywhere proceeds solely for the sake of employing [the object].

However, since a consecration of the form of a rite of performance, once employed, terminates merely in the syllables [of the mantra] and lacks a final consummation in its actual effect, it is inferior.
Therefore, the giving of the staff for the sake of consecrating Maitrāvaruṇa is a primary act (arthakarma).
This being so, even in the case of the Nirūḍhapaśu sacrifice where there is no consecrated person (dīkṣita), this gift is the motivator for the preparation of the staff.
(Regarding the seventh section on the disposal of the Prāsana as a ritual act of dedication, the Sūtra states:

That which is connected with something at its origin is for the sake of that thing, because the scriptural statement is the authority; therefore, when it goes toward another purpose, it should be considered a disposal, since it is a subordinate element. Jaimini 4.2.19.

In the seventh section of the *Mīmāṃsājaiminīya-sūtra* (4.2.14), the author formulates the following inquiry: Is the throwing of a black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit a primary ritual act (*arthakarma*), or [is it a secondary act]?
"Practice [is primary] because it has purpose; the first [is primary], and the last [is primary] due to its utility.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "When the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) have been distributed, he throws the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*) into the Cātvāla pit.
When the ten sacrificial fees have been led away by the sacrificer to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*),...
At that time, the sacrificer should discard the horn of a black antelope, which he has held in his own hand, into the pit named *cātvāla*.
This discarding is a ritual act (*arthakarma*).
Why? Because...

If it is argued that [the statement] is purposeful because it serves as a practice, yet would be meaningless due to the absence of anything previously unknown, and therefore its status as a meaningful action is for the sake of obtaining what was not previously known; [we reply: no.
It is not so;

for by the direct scriptural statement (śruti) of the instrumental case in "he scratches with the black antelope horn," the horn—having been employed for scratching the head of the sacrificer—is dependent upon a disposal (pratipatti).
Nor is there an absolute absence of apūrva in the case of a disposal.

Since a rule such as "the throwing [of the grass] is indeed into the *cātvāla* pit" is mandatory (*vaidha*), even though there is no transcendental result (*apūrva*) produced by the act of throwing itself, there nonetheless exists a transcendental result arising from the observance of the rule.
Therefore, the throwing is a ritual of disposal (*pratipattikarman*).

(Regarding the eighth [topic]: the section on the *avabhṛtha* bath being a *pratipatti-karman*, Sūtras 20–22) And in the case of the Soma sacrifice, it is so because its purpose has been fulfilled. (Jaimini 4.2.20) Or rather, it is a primary act (*arthakarman*), because of its connection with a specific designation. (Jaimini 4.2.21)
Or rather, it is a performance [of the sacrifice], because it follows that logic; thus there is the scriptural mention of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) for the sake of the region.
[Jaimini Sūtra 4.2.22]. The eighth section formulates [the following]:

Regarding the disposal of the Soma-smeared vessel, is its carrying away a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) or a consecratory act (*pratipatti*); for it is heard in scripture that "by means of it [the Soma], they go. (Jaimini Nyāya Mālā 4.2.15)
"Its status as a means [of accomplishment] is not [established] in this way, because the *puroḍāśa* is the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
Since the vessel has no connection with that [oblation], its disposal (*pratipatti*) is for the sake of [its own] final consumption.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "That which is the *ṛjīṣa* (the dregs) of the sacrifice is indeed the fourfold-drawn [portion]."
That which is the pressing-stones,
that which is the Audumbarī post, and that which are the two pressing-boards;
"Therefore, whatever substance is smeared with Soma,
with that they go to the avabhṛtha [concluding bath]. The *ṛjīṣa* is the sapless portion of the Soma that has been squeezed out.
This very substance, such as the *ṛjīṣa* (the dregs) and the pressing stones, becomes smeared with Soma during the pressing and other rites;
it must be accepted that all of this, being thus smeared, serves as the means for the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
Why?

If it is argued that "they go to the *avamṛtha* with that" indicates, through the force of the instrumental case-ending, that the substance smeared with Soma is understood to be the means for the *avamṛtha*,
and therefore that very substance smeared with Soma is taken as the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) for the *avamṛtha*—
it is not so.

Regarding the statement, "They perform the *avabhṛtha* with a cake on one potsherd dedicated to Varuṇa," since the *avabhṛtha* is already occupied by the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) consisting of the cake prescribed in the original injunction (*utpattivākya*), it is impossible for the Soma-smeared vessel to be connected to the *avabhṛtha* as an oblation.
Therefore, the word *avabhṛtha* figuratively indicates the location intended for that rite, and it is the bringing of the Soma-smeared vessel to that location which is enjoined here.
And this bringing serves as a disposal (*pratipatti*).
Because the vessel has already been used previously,
therefore this is an act of disposal (pratipatti-karma).
(Regarding the ninth section on the restrictive purpose of injunctions concerning the agent, place, and time; Sūtras 23–24:

"The agent, place, and time are not subject to injunction because they are eternally inherent in the performance [of the rite]. (Jaimini 4.2.23) "Or rather, the scriptural statement is for the purpose of restriction. (Jaimini 4.2.24)
In the ninth section (adhikaraṇa), he formulates [the inquiry]: "One should sacrifice on level ground; is this a restatement (anuvāda) of place and so forth, or is it an injunction (vidhi)?"
Since the impossibility of practical application has already been established, this is merely a restatement (anuvāda).
The phrase "on even or uneven [ground]" is intended to eliminate the optionality [of the rule].
Here, a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) is prescribed by means of the non-performance of that which was not previously established.
This is recorded in the sacred tradition: "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices on even ground."

"One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva on ground sloping toward the east"; "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day"; "One should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā on the new moon day";

"There are six officiating priests for the Paśubandha sacrifice"; "There are four officiating priests for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices"; "There are five officiating priests for the Cāturmāsya sacrifices"; "There is one [officiating priest] for the Agnihotra sacrifice."
The officiating priest says: "O gentle one, for this sacrificial rite, the seventeen-fold sacrifice, [the injunction is] 'one should sacrifice with Soma'.

The word *kratu* also applies to mental worship (*mānasopāsana*), because in the passage, "He should perform that *kratu*, consisting of mind, having breath as its body," the word *kratu* is used to enjoin meditation (*dhyāna*).
To exclude that [case], the term "non-sacrificial rite" (*ayajña-kratoḥ*) is specified as a qualifier.
In that context, place, time, agent, and materials are not enjoined; rather, they are merely mentioned as already established (*anuśrūyante*).
Why?
Because it has already been attained;
for indeed, an application [of a word] is not possible without [specification of] place and so forth.
If it is argued that its attainment occurs through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*),
it is not so;
