for by means of presumptive testimony, the attainment of the equal portion and so forth is merely optional.
Since uneven ground and other such factors are also possible, therefore,
in that case where [the primary rule] does not apply, even ground and so forth are prescribed.

(Sūtra in the section concerning the restrictive purpose of the injunction of substances and qualities in the tenth [chapter]: "Likewise, in the case of substances, the mention of a quality is for the sake of restriction, because of its connection with the originative injunction. (Jaimini 4.2.25)
The tenth section formulates [the following]:
"Is the mention of the white [animal] a restatement (anuvāda), or is the whiteness the injunction?
Because it is obtained through the medium of the substance, as in the previous case, it is restricted. (MJaiNy 4.2.19)
This is handed down in scripture: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal dedicated to Vāyu.
In that context, since the quality of whiteness cannot be connected to the action independently of a substance, it must be connected to the action only when accompanied by a substance;

and since the substance itself cannot be connected to the action independently [of its qualities], when it is connected as accompanied [by qualities], the prescription of the substance follows as an unavoidable necessity.

If it is argued that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the attainment of that [whiteness], it is not so; for, according to the previous reasoning, it is accepted as an injunction of restriction (*niyamavidhi*) in order to eliminate its optional character (*pākṣikatva*). (MJaiNyC 4.2.19)

(Regarding the eleventh [topic], the section concerning the restrictive purpose of the injunctions for purificatory rites such as *avadhāta*: Sūtra) And in the case of a purificatory rite, because that [substance] is primary. Jaimini 4.2.26.
He formulates the eleventh topic:
"Even in the case of threshing, there is a restrictive rule (niyama) as in the case of [the location] and so forth;
therefore, that [threshing] would be prompted by the primary act, because of the statement regarding its procedure. (MJaiNy 4.2.20)

Just as a restrictive rule is prescribed for place, time, agent, and substance when they might otherwise be optional, so too threshing (avaghāta), although already established by worldly practice for the purpose of producing rice grains, is restricted by injunction to exclude the occasional alternative of splitting them with the fingernails and the like. And since threshing is thus enjoined, it is employed in connection with the primary rite, such as the Āgneya sacrifice.
Nor should it be argued that there is no application [of these rites] here due to a lack of connection;
for their connection is established by virtue of being recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the principal sacrifice.
Therefore, threshing and the other such acts are enjoined and are applied by the principal sacrifice. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 4.2.20)
(Section on the Definition of the Nature of Sacrifice and Oblation in the Twelfth [Chapter], Sūtras 27–28):
"The injunction 'he sacrifices' (yajati) refers to the action involving substance and deity, because its purpose is fulfilled in the aggregate [of these elements]. (Jaimini 4.2.27).
"Since it is heard [in the text] as denoting that [same action], the term 'juhoti' (he offers) should be understood as being the same, with the addition of pouring. (Jaimini 4.2.28).
In the twenty-first to twenty-third sūtras of the fourth book (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra), the twelfth section is formulated as follows:
Are the acts of sacrificing (yāga), offering oblations (homa), and giving (dāna) to be performed without being specifically defined, or are they to be performed after being defined?
The first sacrifice consists of relinquishment; relinquishment is intended as the act of throwing [the offering] into the fire, which is called *homa*.
The expectancy of the word "sacrifice" (yāga) is satisfied solely by its own abandonment;
the injunction of the oblation (homa) following the sacrifice terminates in the act of throwing [the offering].

Giving is the acquisition of another's property by relinquishing one's own; even in the act of renunciation, this is the distinction among these [acts]. This is recorded in the sacred tradition: "One should sacrifice with Soma," "One offers the Agnihotra," and "One gives gold to the Ātreya."
In that regard, the meanings of the words *yāga*, *homa*, and *dāna* cannot be definitively determined,

because the act of relinquishing a substance (*dravyatyāga*) exists in all three. Consequently, since there is no determination of which among the enjoined meanings is the primary one, [the distinction remains unsettled].
If it is argued that, in the other case, the previously mentioned distinction between injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*) would be useless— do not say so.
Sacrifice (*yāga*) is the relinquishing of a substance with reference to a deity.
The casting of what has been relinquished into fire is *homa*.
The giving away of one's own property, preceded by the cessation of one's own ownership and resulting in the production of another's ownership, is *dāna*.
Thus, these categories of things are well-defined.

Since the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta*) is followed by the prescription of the oblation (*homa*)— "he offers the fourfold portion" (*caturavattaṃ juhoti*)— it is understood that "sacrifice" (*yajña*) consists merely of renunciation (*tyāga*), whereas "oblation" (*homa*) is that which includes the act of throwing [the offering] into the fire.
However, where a word such as *yajati* (he sacrifices) is not heard...
However, in the case of the injunction "An eight-potherd [cake] for Agni," only this much is heard;
yet, since both the deity to be designated and the substance to be abandoned are heard therein, the sacrifice—consisting of the form of designation and abandonment—is established by implication.
Therefore, because the sacrifices and other elements to be enjoined as primary are well-defined, the *Vidhiviveka* (Examination of Injunction) is not purposeless.
(Thirteenth Section: On the commonality of the *barhis* grass for the *ātithyā* and other rites; Sūtras 29–30) Sūtra 29:
Because an injunction concludes with the completion of the action, there would be a transfer of the injunction to another purpose.

Sūtra 30: Or rather, because of the connection [of the substance] with its origin, the relationship of the purpose among those that are undifferentiated would be the cause for the unity of performance.
The fourteenth section (adhikaraṇa) [of the fourth chapter] formulates [the following]:
"That the sacrificial grass (barhis) used for the *ātithyā* is extended by analogy (*atideśana*) to the *upasad*s..."
Or rather, the first [alternative] is a rule of general application, because of the subsequent withdrawal of that [general rule].
Because the oneness [of the *barhis*] appears through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the extended application (*atideśa*).
This *barhis* is employed by means of the *ātithyā* and the *upasads*.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard [in the scripture]: "The *barhis* which is used in the *ātithyā*..."
"That [is the rule] for the Upasads, and that for the Agniṣomīya.
Having placed the purchased Soma on the cart, the sacrifice which one performs while facing toward the Prācīnavaṃśa hall during its transport back is this Ātithyā (Guest-offering).
Thereafter, the *upasads* are performed for three days;
on the day of the *aupavasathya*, the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice] is to be performed.
Regarding that, as for the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) prescribed for the *ātithyeṣṭi*:
If, having been taken away from that *iṣṭi*, it were prescribed for the *upasads*, then its prescription in the *ātithyā* would be purposeless.
And if it were prescribed elsewhere after having been used there, [it would likewise be purposeless].
In that case, there would be a contradiction in the form of an already assigned [function] being re-assigned.

Therefore, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached— that the sentence is intended as an extended application (*atideśa*), meaning that those properties belonging to the sacrificial grass of the *ātithyā* offering, such as being horse-hair and so forth, are to be transferred to the *upasad* offerings— [the following is stated]:
We reply: if the word *barhis* were to extend the properties [of one rite] to others, it would entail figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
However, by direct denotation (*śruti*), the oneness of the *barhis* in the Ātithya, Upasad, and Agniṣomīya rites is manifested.
Therefore, what is to be enjoined here is its commonality.

The meaning of the injunctive sentence is that the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) which is procured for the sake of the *ātithyā* rite is not intended solely for the *ātithyā*, but is to be procured for the sake of the *upasad*s and the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice as well.
Therefore, all three— the *ātithyā*, the *upasad*s, and the *agnīṣomīya*— are the motivators (*prayojaka*) for this sacrificial grass.
Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* by the venerable Mādhava.
Now begins the third quarter of the fourth chapter.
(In the first section, concerning the fact that substances, purificatory acts, and ritual actions serve the purpose of the sacrifice, there are Sūtras 1–3.)

In the case of substances, preparatory acts, and rituals, because they exist for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit must be an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). And because the originative injunction does not have that [fruit] as its primary purpose. But the fruit belongs to that [injunction] which has that [fruit] as its primary purpose.
In the third quarter (pāda), the first topic (adhikaraṇa) is formulated as follows:
"Because of the statement that the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood, there is no hearing of evil [consequences], due to its lack of coloring (*añjana*)."
The removal of the gaze of enemies is the armor; what is it for the person by means of the fore-sacrifices?
"Because the fruit does not have the nature of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) for the sake of the ritual action (*kratu*), it does not shine forth as being for the sake of the ritual;
therefore, the fruit must be an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).

This is recorded in the tradition: "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood hears no evil report"; "When he anoints [his eyes], he surely appropriates the eye of his rival"; "When the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are performed, they serve as armor..."
"Indeed, this is performed for the sacrifice;
it is the armor of the sacrificer for the sake of overcoming his rival.
In that context, the material substance is the *parṇa* (palāśa) wood, which serves as the source-material (*prakṛti*) for the *juhū* ladle.
Both that refinement of the eyes by means of collyrium and that armor consisting of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are enjoined as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
Why?
If it is argued that this is because a result pertaining to the person—such as the absence of hearing evil verses and so forth—is manifested [by the Veda], we say:
not so;
for a result is that which is to be accomplished (sādhya).
And here, the state of being a probandum (sādhyatā) does not appear; [as in the examples:
"he hears," "he eats," "armor is made."

Because of this indication of present tense, these injunctions are for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). In that regard, although the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood (*parṇamayītva*) is taught as an independent rule (*anārabhyādhīta*), its connection with the sacrifice is established by syntactical statement (*vākya*).

Regarding the *saṃskāra* (purificatory) and *varman* (protective) rites, however, because they are for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), there is no expectation of a fruit apart from the accomplishment of the sacrifice; therefore, even by transforming the present-tense indication into another tense, it is impossible to postulate a fruit.
Consequently, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—consisting of such things as the absence of hearing ill-repute—is the cause for the misconception that these rites possess a fruit.

(Regarding the second section [adhikaraṇa] on the impermanent nature of the purpose of occasional rites, the sūtra states: "In the case of an occasional rite, because it is a modification, another [act] should be the primary element of the sacrifice.
(Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.4)

The second section formulates the argument: "One who desires [a specific result] should bring [the water] in an earthen vessel; but is this also the case for the obligatory rite, or something else? Since there is both expectancy and proximity, the earthen vessel applies even to the obligatory rite. (MJaiNy_4.3.3)

Because it serves the purpose of desire, there is an unfitness [for the obligatory]; and since the expectancy is satisfied by that which is prescribed as general, the other would be for the sake of the obligatory. Even though the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) is invariably connected with the act "he carries forward the water," the means of accomplishment is indeed an earthen vessel.
It has been established [that this is so],

because even in the case of something eternal, there is no requirement for it to be a "receptacle" (pātra). Nor should it be argued that some [receptacle] established by worldly convention is being adopted here.

Since, in the case of a rite not explicitly mentioned [in the context], that which is mentioned elsewhere is proximate— this being the position reached— we reply: earthenware vessels are prescribed for the sake of desire,
and they are appropriate when such a desire exists.
For that which proceeds by taking a partial desire as its motive is not suitable for what is permanent.
However, the desire for a vessel is satisfied by that which is prescribed in a general manner;
for the injunction "he brings forward water" is prescribed without specifying a particular vessel.

Since the substitute is established as something else through the impossibility of otherwise [accomplishing the rite], it is conceived as being similar to that original vessel in some general respect.
Therefore, in the case of constant performance (*nityaprayoga*), that optional (*kāmya*) earthen vessel does not follow; rather, any other vessel whatsoever should be employed.
If it is argued that "one should bring water with a *camasa* (ladle)" thus prescribes the vessel for the obligatory rite,
then let this be considered a *kṛtvācintā* (a hypothetical discussion).
(Third [section]: On the principle of conjunction and separation; in the section concerning the dual purpose—both constant and occasional—of curd and other such items, Sūtras 5–7.)
But when one thing serves both purposes, there is the principle of "separateness through conjunction" (saṃyogapṛthaktva). [Objection:
"It is a subsidiary (śeṣa)," if this is argued. [Reply:
No, because the purposes are distinct.
Now, the third section begins:
"But [the injunction] 'with curd for one desiring sensory power'— is this [curd] part of the obligatory rite, or is it something else?"

"It might be otherwise as before; it is not so, because of the distinctness of the conjunction. (MJaiNy 4.3.5) In the Agnihotra, it is heard: "One desiring sensory power should offer with curd. In that case, since the curd is a different [element], it should not be employed in the obligatory Agnihotra according to the previous principle.
If it is argued that it is some entirely different substance,
this is not so;
for in the other sentence, "One offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), having introduced the connection with a specific desire, curd is prescribed in connection with the obligatory (*nitya*) oblation.
Therefore, even for a single substance such as curd, its obligatory nature and its optional (kāmya) nature are not contradictory when expressed by two separate sentences.

Similarly, in the case of the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, the following should be cited as examples: "He binds [the animal] to a post made of Khadira wood" and "One desiring virility should make the sacrificial post (yūpa) of Khadira wood. MJaiNyC_4,3.5 //

(Regarding the fourth section on the nature of the milk-vow and other observances as being duties of the sacrifice, Sūtras 8–9: "But for substances intended for ritual action, the consecration should be a duty of the sacrifice" (Jaimini 4.3.8).
"Because of their distinctness, it should remain restricted [to each]" (Jaimini 4.3.9).
The fourth section (adhikaraṇa) begins with the verse: "Is the milk-vow for the Brāhmaṇa intended for his gender, or rather for that specific ritual act?"

"Do not say that [the milk] is for the sake of the man; rather, because it is fruitless [as a human goal], it is a subsidiary of the sacrifice."—In the Jyotiṣṭoma, regarding the absence of food for one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*), a vow (*vrata*) is prescribed: "Milk is the vow for a Brāhmaṇa, gruel (*yavāgū*) for a Rājanya..."

Regarding the statement, "The curd-mixture (āmikṣā) is for the Vaiśya," if it is argued that this vow is for the sake of the person because of its connection with persons such as Brāhmaṇas and others,
it is not so.
Because the fruit is not mentioned here— as it is in the case of the sense organs, vigor, and so forth—
the status of being a subsidiary to the sacrifice (*kratūśeṣatva*) is understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Brāhmaṇas and other types of persons are introduced as causal conditions (*nimitta*) for the determination of specific materials.
(Regarding the fifth section, contained within the Viśvajit-nyāya, concerning the topic that the Viśvajit and other such sacrifices possess fruit—Sūtras 10–12:

"Since no fruit is heard mentioned in the injunction, only the ritual act itself would be enjoined; for that which is not expressed by the word is not understood [from it]. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.10) "Or rather, by the force of the traditional text (āmnāna), it should be understood through the purpose of the injunction. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.11)
For words are understood through the meaningfulness of their referents;
for those that are semantically incapable [of connection], there is no relation even when they are in immediate proximity. Therefore, it is a partial expression of the direct statement (*śruti*).
And the meaning of the sentence is like that of a subordinate element (*guṇa*). (Jaimini 4.3.11–12)

In the fifth section of the fourth chapter of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra, [the author] formulates the following: "Is there no fruit at all in the Viśvajit sacrifice, or is there one? [The prima facie view is: There is none, because it is not heard [in scripture]."
Since an injunction requires something to be brought about, a fruit must be postulated for the sake of a person’s engagement [in the rite].
Regarding this, it is traditionally taught: "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit.
If it is argued that there is no fruit for the Viśvajit sacrifice because no fruit is mentioned therein—
Not so;
for the result must be postulated.
The efficient force (*bhāvanā*) expressed by the statement "one should effect [something] by means of the sacrifice named Viśvajit" requires an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*).

Because the expectancy, "What should one do? remains unfulfilled, some fruit must necessarily be supplied to complete the sentence. Once that [fruit] is supplied, the performance of the sacrifice is established through the engagement of a person who desires it.
Otherwise, because there would be no one entitled [to perform it], the injunction regarding its performance would be purposeless.
Therefore, a fruit must be postulated.
(Regarding the sixteenth topic, contained within the *Viśvajit-nyāya*, concerning the section on the single fruit of the *Viśvajit* and other sacrifices, Sūtras 13–14:
"That [sacrifice] is for all purposes, because there is no specific instruction. (Jaimini 4.3.13)
"Or [it is] one, because the injunction is one. (Jaimini 4.3.14). He formulates the sixth section as follows:

Should there be every fruit or only one? Let it be everything, since there is no distinction; by means of one [sacrifice], that [desire] is fulfilled, and therefore a plurality [of fruits] is not postulated.
In that Viśvajit sacrifice, everything—such as cattle, sons, virility, and sensory power—is to be postulated as the fruit.
If it is argued: "Why?
Because there is no specific reason [to establish] that 'this alone is its fruit,'" do not say so.
Because lightness alone is the specific cause [of the action].

(Regarding the seventh [topic], within the *viśvajit-nyāya*, concerning the section on the heaven as the fruit of the *viśvajit* and other sacrifices, Sūtras 15–16: "That [fruit] shall be heaven, because it is common to all;
and because of the [scriptural] cognition. (Jaimini 4.3.15–16)
Now, the seventh section (adhikaraṇa) of the Mīmāṃsājaiminīya-sūtra-vṛtti (MJaiNy) 4.3.9 formulates [the following]:
Is it any single thing whatsoever, or is it restricted? There is no restrictive rule.
Therefore, since it is desired by all men, heaven alone is that [result].
If it is argued: "When a single result is being postulated for the Viśvajit sacrifice, there is no restrictive rule that it must be this one or that;
therefore, if any particular result were to be postulated according to someone's desire, then—since the result would effectively be everything—it would involve unnecessary complexity (gaurava)."
Not so;
because heaven, unlike fruits such as cattle and the like, is not mixed with suffering,
and because it is desired by all persons due to its being unsurpassed bliss, heaven alone is the fruit of the Viśvajit sacrifice.

(Regarding the eighth section on the principle of the Rātrisatra sacrifice, specifically the section concerning the fact that the Rātrisatra has its fruit based on an explanatory passage [arthavāda], Sūtras 17–19: Kārṣṇājini maintains that in the case of a sacrifice, the explanatory passage regarding the fruit is like an auxiliary [aṅga].
Ātreya holds that the fruit [is established] because of the explicit instruction; for where it is not heard, there must be inference. Jaim_4.3.17–18.
The praise [of the limbs] is for the sake of another, because it serves a different purpose. (Jaimini 4.3.19).
The eighth section formulates [the following]:—
"Whether for the sake of heaven or for stability, the Rātrisatra is the first here;
it should be like the previous case, and stability is heard [in scripture], which is better than what is not heard.
In the section on Satras, it is heard regarding each one: "These indeed become established..."
"Those who perform these nights [become endowed with splendor]," and "Those who perform these [become] possessed of Vedic luster and eaters of food."

All those specific *satra* sacrifices that occur after twelve days— such as the thirteen-night (*trayodaśarātra*), fourteen-night (*caturdaśarātra*), and so forth— are designated by a singular ending, generally referring to the collective whole. For instance, a specific *satra* sacrifice in which there are three nights characterized by the number thirteen is called "the thirteen-night [sacrifice]," where the singular form is used because the aggregate is the primary referent.

In some instances, however, the nights are mentioned by the word "rātri. For example: "He saw these twenty nights. Regarding such a Rātrisatra sacrifice, it might be argued that, according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice, heaven (svarga) must be postulated as the fruit.
To this we reply: in the explanatory passage (arthavāda) which serves as a praise for this injunction of the Rātrisatra, "firm foundation" (pratiṣṭhā) is heard [as the result].
And in this statement, that [result] is much closer than heaven, which is not mentioned at all.
Therefore, one must conceive of "firm standing" (*pratiṣṭhā*) itself as the fruit, as in: "One desiring firm standing should perform the Rātri-sattra."
(Ninth Adhikaraṇa: On the fact that optional rites yield the stated optional fruits;
Sūtras 20–24) In an optional rite, heaven is the constant result, just as in a subsidiary of a sacrifice, it serves the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*).
(Jaimini 4.3.20) And because [the fruit] is restricted once the cause has ceased. (Jaimini 4.3.21)
Or rather, desire is enjoined through its connection with that [the sacrifice],
because it is subordinate to the subsidiary (Jaimini 4.3.22);
and when [the result] has ceased, there is a restriction for that purpose (Jaimini 4.3.23–24).

The eleventh section (adhikaraṇa) of the fourth chapter of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra formulates [the following]: Is it the heard or the unheard [mantra] that is used? Only the heard one, for the sake of universal application in the Saurya sacrifice.
The first [view] says: "Not so; for by the scriptural statement itself, the desire for a fruit is averted.
In the case of the injunction, "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya," spiritual luster is the explicitly stated fruit (*śruta-phala*).
Heaven (*svarga*) is the unstated fruit (*aśruta-phala*).
Both of these [objections] must be accepted.
If that were so, since heaven is desired by all, it might be argued that everyone would consequently engage in [the means to attain] it.
But this is not the case.

Since the scriptural statement is already free from expectancy by virtue of the fruit consisting of Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*), it is impossible to assume a fruit such as heaven according to the *Viśvajit* principle;
therefore, the fruit is indeed that which is explicitly stated in the scripture.

(Tenth [Adhikaraṇa], within the section on the logic of the Darśapūrṇamāsa: On the point that the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites serve the purpose of all desires; Sūtras 25–26) Sūtra 25: All that is desired [is obtained] through the desires for the subsidiaries, because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Sūtra 26: Or rather, it is the teaching of the fruit [of the primary rite itself], because of its connection with the word denoting the principal [action].

In the tenth section of the *Mīmāṃsājaiminīya-sūtravṛtti*, he formulates [the following]: Is the Darśa and other sacrifices a restatement (*anuvāda*) for all desires, or is it an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding the result?
Desire arising from the primary and secondary limbs is restated because of the absence of a scriptural injunction.

Relying on the establishment of the injunction for origination (*utpatticodanā*) through the [concepts of] ritual procedure (*vidhi*) and creative realization (*bhāvanā*), this [injunction] becomes an injunction regarding the fruit (*phale vidhi*) by means of the cognition of its connection with the result.
This is recited in the scripture: "The other sacrifices are performed for the sake of a single desire..."
"The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices [are performed] for the sake of all [desires]," and "Other sacrificial rites are undertaken for the sake of one specific desire,
but the Jyotiṣṭoma is for the sake of all."
In this regard, by the sentence "for all [results]," there is no injunction regarding the fruit of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
for there is an absence of an injunctive suffix (liṅ) or the like, as well as an absence of a verb expressive of productive activity (bhāvanā).
Rather, it will be a restatement (anuvāda).
This is because all desires have been attained.
Nor should it be argued that, since the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" prescribes heaven alone, no other desire is attained;
for even the desires for the primary and subsidiary components [of the sacrifice] have likewise been attained.

The *sāmidhenī* verses are an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). In that context, specific desires are mentioned: "One desiring stability should recite twenty-one;
one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should recite twenty-four."
Likewise, milking is an auxiliary (aṅga) of the Sāṃnāyya sacrifice;
the driving away of the calf, which is the means for that milking, is a sub-auxiliary (upāṅga).
In that context, a desire is prescribed regarding the fetching of a Palāśa branch: "He who should desire, 'May I be possessed of cattle'—"
"One should bring for him a tree with many leaves and many branches; this makes him truly possessed of cattle"— thus,
when it is argued that all these desires are merely being restated (anūdyante), [the following is said]:

We reply: Even if there be no injunction or productive operation (*bhāvanā*) in this sentence, nevertheless, by relying on the fact that it is established as an originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), the connection with the fruit is understood through the dative case (*caturthī*) which expresses "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*).
Therefore, this is an injunction regarding the fruit.

(Regarding the eleventh [section], contained within the *darśapūrṇamāsa-nyāya*, concerning the section on the separate performance of the *darśa*, *pūrṇamāsa*, and other rites for their respective fruits, and the *yogasiddhi-nyāya*, Sūtras 27–28:
"In that case, all [fruits follow from each rite] because there is no distinction. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.27)
"Or rather, there is the accomplishment of yoga, because the purpose is not connected with origination.
(Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.28). [The author] formulates the eleventh section as follows:

And the Jyotiṣṭoma serves all purposes; since everything is accomplished by its performance once, it should yield [the result] either through separate performances or, because there is no distinction regarding it, by being performed once.
For indeed, it is enjoined that each individual result is to be accomplished by its own specific means;
therefore, these desires come to be fulfilled in succession.
Just as the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices are intended for the sake of all desires, [so too is the case here].
Likewise, it has already been established by the preceding section that the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is for the sake of all desires;
in both cases, the desires are contingent (naimittika),
while the essential nature of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites is fixed.
And that [cause] is common to all desires;
for when the cause is shared in common, there can be no alternation among the effects resulting from it,
since we do not observe an alternation between burning and illumination when in proximity to fire.
Therefore, since it is impossible to prevent other results from arising just as one result is accomplished when the Jyotiṣṭoma is performed once, all results would be achieved simultaneously—
this being the prima facie view, we reply: desires are not enjoined by making the Jyotiṣṭoma the occasion for their fulfillment.

Because desires are not themselves to be performed, what then? The Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is enjoined solely as a means for the sake of those desires which are already obtained by a person spontaneously.
Although, in the phrase "for all desires," it appears that there is a requirement for simultaneity because the fruits such as heaven and cattle are denoted by a single word, [this is not the case].
Nevertheless, that [concomitance] does not exist here, because concomitance (*sāhitya*) is not intended to be expressed since it resides in the subject (*uddeśya*).
Nor should it be argued that even if there is no verbal restriction of concomitance, concomitance exists by implication (*arthataḥ*) because they share a single action and result.
Because heaven, cattle, and so forth are each fruits independently of one another,
action is enjoined as the means for each individual fruit.
For this very reason, the designation "for all" is logically justified.
Otherwise, due to the rule of *sāhitya* (conjunction), these would result in only a single combined fruit, and thus the word "all" (*sarva*) would be untenable.
Therefore, whenever a particular fruit is desired, at that time the Jyotiṣṭoma must be performed for the sake of accomplishing it.
Whenever even a single result, such as good rain, is desired, the Kārīrī sacrifice is performed again and again;
what need is there to mention that when the results differ, the performance must differ?
Therefore, there is a separate performance for each individual result.

In the twelfth [book], in the section on the optional rites (kāmyāni) which possess fruits both in this world and the next, under sūtras 27–28, there is another interpretation (*varṇaka*) stating: "In that case, all those [rites] [should be performed] without distinction. (MJaiNyC 4.3.27)
Or rather, there is the accomplishment of yoga, because the purpose is not connected with its production.

In the twelfth adhikaraṇa of the fourth chapter of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra (4.3.16–17), [the author] formulates the following: "Are the cattle resulting from the Citrā sacrifice restricted to that very [next] life, or not?"
The first [is so called] because it is equal to heaven and because it produces the body.
But regarding the production of a variegated result, there is neither a scriptural injunction nor a logical postulation [of a restrictive rule].
When the obstacle [to the result] has been removed by the activity of the person and so forth, the fruit would come to be.

Desirable rites (*kāmyakarman*) are heard in scripture as follows: "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citri* [offering]," and "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra."
In this regard, just as it is certain that the fruit of heaven belongs to the next world (*amuṣmika*),
so too is the fruit of cattle and the like.
If the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, which is the cause of heaven, were the producer of another body, [then the same would apply].
If it is argued that the painting and so forth should likewise be so,
it is not thus,
because of the disparity.

Since it is impossible for one to experience heaven in this very body, the production of another body, though not explicitly stated in scripture, is inferred through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
However, there is no scriptural rule stating that "another body must necessarily be produced by the Citrā sacrifice," nor is there anything else that warrants such an inference.

If it is argued that since the fruit consisting of cattle and so forth can be enjoyed even with this very body, and since cattle and such are not obtained in this life without visible means such as receiving gifts, therefore the fruit of the *vaidha-citra* sacrifice and others must be exclusively for the next world— this is not so;
for receiving gifts and the like are merely useful for the removal of obstacles.
Therefore—when there is no obstacle, the result is of this world; but when there is an obstacle, it belongs to the next world.

(Thirteenth Section: On the Subordination of the Sautrāmaṇī and Other Rites to the Cayanādi; Sūtras 29–31) Because the connection with the injunction is meaningful in the case of a combination [of rites], [the Sautrāmaṇī is subordinate]. Jaimini 4.3.29.
If it is argued that, when there is a mention of time, it refers to time [and not subordination], Jaimini 4.3.30.
"It would not [apply] because of the lack of non-inherence with the purpose. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.31).
The thirteenth section (adhikaraṇa) is formulated as follows:
But having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should perform the Bṛhaspatisava;
or rather, it should be understood that the statement serves as an indicator of its [the Vājapeya’s] subsidiary status.
"The temporal sequence appears here due to the hearing of the suffix *ktvā*; do not say so, for there is the cognition of subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*).

Direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is primary, and the ritual context (*prakriyā*) is likewise favored when that is the case. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 4.3.19) This is recorded in the sacred tradition: "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava."
"One who, having piled the fire-altar (āgniciti), should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī.
In this regard, the suffix *ktvā* in the word "having sacrificed" (*iṣṭvā*) expresses that the Vājapeya occurs at a prior time.
Therefore, it follows that this sentence teaches that the Bṛhaspatisava occurs subsequent to the Vājapeya—this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
We reply: The primary meaning of the *ktvā* suffix here is precisely to convey that the Bṛhaspatisava is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Vājapeya;
for by the Pāṇinian sūtra "When two actions have the same agent, [the suffix is used] for the earlier time" (3.4.21), it is prescribed when there is a single agent for two actions.
Although it is stated in the Sūtra that "it refers to a time prior [to the action]," this is not necessarily fixed,
because in the expression "he sleeps with his mouth open," such usage occurs even when there is identity of time.
The context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Vājapeya sacrifice is also supported by its being an auxiliary (*aṅga*).
Otherwise, since the time [of the Bṛhaspatisava] would be prescribed for something not part of the primary context, the context would be sublated.

If it is argued that "if it were an auxiliary, the word *tat* (that) would be inappropriate because there would be no connection with the Bṛhaspatisava as a distinct ritual well-known [independently]," we say: no.
Because, according to the principle of the *māsāgnihotra*, this serves to extend (*atideśa*) those specific characteristics [of the model sacrifice].
Therefore, this sentence is intended to convey [the status of] being an auxiliary (*aṅga*).
The same construction should be applied here even to the phrase "having piled the fire-altar" (*agniṃ citvā*).
(Section 14: On the subordination of the Baimṛdha and other rites to the Full Moon sacrifice and others;
Sūtras 32–35) “If it be argued that [the rite] serves both purposes,” [Sūtra 32].
“No, because of the unity of the scriptural injunction,” [Sūtra 33].
If it is argued that [the application] is due to the context (*prakaraṇa*), [we reply]: No, because of the connection with the original injunction (*utpatti-saṃyoga*). (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.35)

The fourteenth section formulates the problem: Having established the Full Moon sacrifice, the Vaimṛdha [offering] is prescribed in its wake; is it an auxiliary to both sacrifices or to only one? It should belong to both, by virtue of the context. (Mīmāṃsā Nyāya Bindu 4.3.20)

Because of the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) and because of the manifestation of a connection (*saṃyoga*), [the *vaimṛdha* offering] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Full Moon sacrifice (*pūrṇamāsa*) alone, and not of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*); for the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside by the direct statement (*vākya*).
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, it is heard in scripture: "Having completed the Full Moon sacrifice, one subsequently offers the *vaimṛdha*."

If it is argued that this Baimṛdha offering, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to both the New and Full Moon sacrifices—just like the *prayāja* offerings and others—we say no; for the direct syntactical statement (*vākya*) is more powerful.
Nor should it be said that its being an auxiliary to the Full Moon sacrifice is improper because the word "having concluded" (*saṃsthāpya*) denotes the completion of the Full Moon sacrifice.
This is because that [interpretation] is logical on the basis of the intention to complete the subsidiaries common to the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*).

Therefore, due to the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) and the suffix *ktvā* which expresses a single agent, it is a subsidiary of the Full Moon sacrifice (*pūrṇamāsa*) alone. (MJaiNyC 4.3.20–21)
(Fifteenth [adhikaraṇa] – Sūtra on the point that the *anuyāja* offerings and others occur after the *āgnimāruta* litany:
"But when there is no [independent] origination, it would be a matter of time, because of its connection with a purpose. Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.36.

He formulates the fifteenth topic for discussion: Should one perform the after-offerings (anuyājas) after the Āgnimāruta [offering], or is time an auxiliary (aṅga)? Otherwise, there would be excessive subordination (atipārārthya).
Previously, it was understood that this [offering] to Agni and Marut has Soma as its purpose;
likewise, the after-offerings (anuyājas) have the animal sacrifice as their purpose, while the conjunction [of these elements] is for the sake of establishing the proper time.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard in scripture: "One proceeds with the after-offerings after the offering to Agni and Marut."
The *āgnimāruta-śastra* is a particular liturgical recitation (*śastra*).
The *anuyājas* are the oblations performed with the eleven mantras beginning with "devaṃ barhiḥ," which are recited in the section on animal sacrifice (*pāśuka-hautraka-kāṇḍa*).

In this context, the connection [between them] is intended to make known the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), namely: "the *anuyājas* are subordinate to the *āgnimāruta-śastra*."
If this were an instruction regarding the time for the after-offerings (anuyājas), then the mention of the Āgnimāruta would have no purpose of its own; thus, it would be entirely extraneous.
Therefore, like the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice—
Just as in the case of the Vaimṛdha [offering],
when it is argued that the after-offerings (anuyājas) are a subsidiary part [of the Soma sacrifice],
we reply: like other stotras and śastras, the Agnimāruta-śastra has already been understood previously to be a subsidiary part of the Soma sacrifice.

In the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) dedicated to Agni and Soma, it is understood—by extension (atideśa)—that the eleven after-offerings (anuyāja), like the principal sacrifice itself, are subsidiary parts of the animal sacrifice (paśu).
Therefore, since a mutual relationship of principal and subsidiary between them is impossible, this conjunction is intended to prescribe the time.
(Regarding the sixteenth [topic]—the section concerning the fact that the Soma sacrifice and others follow the New and Full Moon sacrifices; the sūtra:
"In a matter concerning the time of origin, it should be a time [rule], because the sentence has that as its primary purpose. (Jaimini 4.3.37)
The sixteenth section formulates the problem:

Is there a relationship of primary and subordinate between the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and the Soma sacrifice, or is it merely a matter of time? For [the latter] would constitute subordination only for the sake of avoiding purposelessness. (MJaiNy 4.3.24)
The Soma sacrifice is enjoined at a time characterized by the Darśa and other [Full Moon] sacrifices;
because it possesses its own independent fruit, it is not logical for those two [the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa and the Soma] to stand in the relationship of primary and subsidiary (aṅga-aṅgin).
This is recorded in the scripture: "Having sacrificed with the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with the Soma."

If it is argued that— since neither of the two [the new and full moon sacrifices] is dependent on the other, as is the case with the *āgnimāruta* and the *anuyāja* offerings— the conjunction [of Soma with the new and full moon sacrifices] is intended to establish Soma’s status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the Darśapūrṇamāsa, in order to avoid the fault of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) as stated in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa— this is not so.
Because it is impossible for Soma—which possesses its own independent fruit—to be a subordinate member [of another rite], according to the maxim:

"In proximity to that which possesses a fruit, that which lacks a fruit becomes its subordinate member. Nor can it be argued here that, by the logic of the Bṛhaspati-sava, a separate ritual action with its own fruit is enjoined as having the same characteristics as the Soma sacrifice.
Since the word *soma* lacks the status of being subordinate to the word *bṛhaspatisava*, it cannot serve as a transmitter of ritual characteristics (*dharmātideśaka*).
Furthermore, the suffix *-ktvā* is justified by the mere identity of the agent even in the absence of a relationship between principal and subordinate acts.
Therefore, even if one accepts that the word *darśapūrṇamāsa* exists for the sake of another, this injunction regarding the *soma* sacrifice refers to the subsequent time indicated by that *iṣṭi*.
With this very intention, its nature as a chariot is recorded in scripture: "The New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed the chariot of the gods.
He who, having sacrificed with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, then sacrifices with Soma, stands at the end of the chariot-path, in the excellent abode of the gods.
Here, "avasāne" means in the determined [destination].
"On the excellent path" means that just as a traveler experiences ease on a road worn smooth by chariots due to the absence of afflictions such as thorns and stones,

so too for one who has first performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the performance of ritual duties in subsequent modified forms (vikṛti) of those sacrifices— such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā and Prāyaṇīyā rites which are auxiliary to the Soma sacrifice— becomes easy. This is the meaning.
Therefore, the conjunction has time as its purpose.
(Seventeenth [topic], within the section concerning the Vaiśvānara sacrifice performed as a *jāteṣṭi*:

Sūtras 38–39) "But there would be no connection with the fruit if it were not enjoined, because it is not a subordinate element. (Jaimini 4.3.38) "However, the connection of the subsidiaries with injury is for the purpose of an occasion. (Jaimini 4.3.39)

In the seventeenth adhikaraṇa of the fourth chapter of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra (4.3.26–27), [the author] formulates the following: "Regarding the Vaiśvānara-iṣṭi, does the state of being purified belong to the father or the son? The former [is correct]."
The fruit belongs to the agent alone; for agency indeed belongs to the father himself.
Upon the birth of one for whom he should offer this sacrifice, that [son] becomes purified;
and because that desired result belongs to the father, the father proceeds therein.

In the section on optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi-kāṇḍa*), having introduced the rule, "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born," it is heard: "Upon the birth of which [son] one offers this sacrifice, that very [son] becomes purified, resplendent, an eater of food, and possessed of sensory power."
"In this regard,
the agency belongs to the father who has awakened, and not to the son who is in a state of swoon."
If it is argued that, in order to avoid the fault of the action and its result having different loci (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), the fruit such as purification must belong to the father alone—
this is not so; for by the sentence, "He who, upon whose birth he offers [the sacrifice], is purified," the connection of the fruit with the son is understood.
And it should not be argued that, in this case, the father would not engage in the rite because it is fruitless for him;
for since the son’s attainment of purity and so forth is what is desired, it is possible for him to engage in the action with the thought that it is his own fruit.
Therefore, [the result] such as the son's purity belongs to the son.

(Regarding the eighteenth section, which falls within the discussion on the *vaiśvānareṣṭi* sacrifice performed after the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), the same sūtra has been stated under another interpretation:
"But the connection of the subsidiary rites with [the father's] affliction is for the purpose of [indicating] the occasion. (MJaiNyC 4.3.31)
Starting with *Mīmāṃsājaiñī* 4.3.28–29,
the eighteenth section (adhikaraṇa) is formulated as follows: "Is the *iṣṭi* sacrifice to be performed immediately after birth, or once the *jātakarman* rite has been completed?"
The effect follows immediately after the cause; therefore, it is the subsequent [element], being the "caused" (naimittika).

Since the consumption of breast milk is observed once the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) has been completed, that [offering] should take place after the child’s death, even before the *iṣṭi* sacrifice. This is because the birth of a son is the specific occasion for the *vaiśvānareṣṭi*.
If it is argued that because there can be no delay for one who acts according to a specific cause, the attainment occurs immediately after birth—
this is not so.
The feeding with breast milk is prescribed immediately after the birth-rite (*jātakarman*).
If the Vaiśvānara sacrifice were to be performed even before the birth-rite,
then because of the extreme delay in the feeding with breast milk, the son would perish.

If that were the case, to whom would the desired fruit of the sacrifice, such as purification and so forth, belong? Therefore, it is not immediately after birth, but rather the sacrifice takes place after the *jātakarman* (birth-rite).

(Regarding the nineteenth [topic], within the section concerning the principle of the Jāteṣṭi sacrifice, in the discussion on the Vaiśvānareṣṭi being performed after the cessation of impurity, the same Sūtra is stated under a different interpretation:
"But the connection of the subsidiaries with the occurrence of an injury is for the purpose of [establishing] the occasion. (Mīmāṃsā-Jaimini-Nyāya-Candrikā 4.3.39)
Now, the nineteenth section (adhikaraṇa) of the fourth chapter on the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras formulates the following:
Should the *jātakarman* (birth rite) take place immediately after birth, or once the period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) has passed?
The first [is for the sake of] the proximity of the occasion; the latter is for the sake of the purity of the agent.

Even though birth—which serves as the occasion for its performance—is proximate immediately after the *jātakarma*, nevertheless, if it were performed by a father who is impure, it would be deficient in its constituent parts (*aṅga*).
However, regarding the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), a temporary purification for the sake of avoiding misfortune has been shown by the scripture itself.

Therefore, because the presence of the primary [element] necessarily takes precedence, one should perform the *iṣṭi* sacrifice after the period of impurity (*āśauca*) has passed, in order to prevent a deficiency in the auxiliary factor characterized by purification.
(Regarding the section on the performance of various subsidiary elements of the Sautrāmaṇī and other rites at their own times, Sūtras 40–41):
Because of the connection with the principal rite, the subsidiaries have the time of the principal.
But since [the principal] has not yet commenced, there is an injunction; because of that commonality, it should take place at its own time. (Jaimini 4.3.40–41)
The twenty-first section (viṃśādhikaraṇa) is formulated as follows:
"Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī"— is such a sacrifice an auxiliary (aṅga)?
Whether it occurs at the time of its own subsidiary or at its own [independent] time, the first [type] is considered to be like other subsidiaries.
But when the piling [of the fire-altar] and other such rites have been completed, because another rite is enjoined,
its performance is established at its own time as obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction).

Regarding the statements, "Having piled the fire, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī" and "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," the status of the Sautrāmaṇī and the Bṛhaspatisava as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) has already been stated previously.
If it is argued that "that subsidiary must be employed together with the principal at the time of the principal,
because the other subsidiaries are employed in that manner," it is not so.

Because the *sautrāmaṇī* and other rites are prescribed as distinct subsequent actions once the principal rite, such as the *cayana*, has been completed along with its subsidiaries— this being expressed by the *ktvā* suffix which denotes priority of time—
if there were a single performance (*ekaprayoga*) together with the principal rite,
then the distinction between prior and posterior time established by the *ktvā* suffix would be sublated.

For it is not heard in scripture that the implements such as the sacrificial ladles and vessels, which are to be employed together with the principal rite (*aṅgin*), are to be enjoined after the *cayana* (piling of the altar) has been completed; rather, since their separate performance is necessarily required, their execution is proper when they are brought forth by their respective injunctive rules (*codaka*).
Furthermore, because the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice has the *iṣṭi* as its archetype, the time for the parvan (the new or full moon) is obtained by extension (*atideśa*).

If, however, there were a single performance together with the *cayana* (the piling of the fire-altar), then because the preparation of the *ukhā* (fire-pan) and other rites are prescribed for the *parvan* (the full moon or new moon day), the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice would be restricted to that other day. Likewise, since the *bṛhaspatisava* is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the spring season is obtained for it by the force of the archetypal injunction (*codaka*).
If there were a unity of performance with the Vājapeya, then since the Vājapeya is prescribed for the autumn season, the Bṛhaspatisava would also necessarily fall in the autumn.
Therefore, its performance takes place in the spring, following that [Vājapeya] on a transferred (atidiṣṭa) lunar day.
But surely, in all cases, the transcendental result of the primary rite (*pradhānāpūrva*) must be produced by the transcendental results of the auxiliary rites (*aṅgāpūrva*).

If it is argued that, since the *phalāpūrva* (the unseen potency of the fruit) has already been produced here by the prior performance of the principal rite together with its subsidiaries, the subsequent subsidiary is therefore purposeless—[we reply:
no, for it must be understood that this very *apūrva* attains a state of intensity through this particular subsidiary.
Therefore, there is no performance [of the subsidiary] at the time of the principal rite.
But it is established that [the performance occurs] at its own time. // MJaiNyC 4.3.31–32 //
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* by the venerable Mādhava.
Now begins the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter.
(In the first section, concerning whether the sacrifices in the Rājasūya have gambling and other acts as their constituent parts, Sūtras 1–2:)
Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.1: On account of the commonality of the word *prakaraṇa* (context), the injunctions [of the subsidiaries] do not constitute parts [of the main sacrifice].
Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.2: Or rather, they should be parts, because they are distinguished from non-sacrificial acts.

In the first section of the fourth quarter, he formulates the following: "In the Rājasūya, both the Anumati and other offerings and the gambling and other rites—are these two primary acts, or is there primacy for only one? The first [position] holds because of the unity of the context. (MJaiNy 4.4.1)
Because they constitute the *rājasūya*, the sacrifices possess the status of primary acts (*aṅgin*) due to their connection with a fruit;
whereas that which is fruitless, such as the gambling and so forth, is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the fruitful sacrifice.
In the context of the *rājasūya*, many sacrifices in the form of offerings are heard in scripture, such as: "To Anumati, a cake on eight potsherds... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.8.1).
"He offers a cake on one potsherd to Nirṛti," "He offers a caru-oblation to Āditya," "A cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu," and so forth.
Just as these *iṣṭis* (sacrificial offerings) are prescribed, so too are animal sacrifices (*paśus*) heard in the scripture: "One should immolate a dew-lapped, pregnant ewe for Āditya."
"‘The speckled one for Māruta,’ ‘the four-year-old female for the Aśvins,’ and so forth.
*Malhā* means *maṇilā*, that is to say, one possessing a dewlap and udders; Aditi is its deity."
The *pṛśni* is one with a small body;
its presiding deity is the Maruts.
To whatever extent of age—in the form of three years—there arises the capacity to carry a burden on its back, [to that extent it is the *pṛśni*].
A four-year-old cow that has not yet calved is its [the sacrifice's] sacrificial animal;
the Aśvins are its deities.
In this manner, the Soma sacrifices such as the Abhiṣecanīya and the Daśapeya are prescribed in the Śruti.
Likewise, there are *darvihomas* such as "the offering in the anthill" (*valmīkavapāyāṃ homaḥ*).

Just as these four types—*iṣṭi*, animal sacrifice (*paśu*), *soma*, and *darvihoma*—are of the nature of sacrifice (*yāga*), so too are gambling and other such acts heard of in scripture as being non-sacrificial in nature, such as: "He plays with a four-year-old mare," "He plays with dice," "He defeats a Kṣatriya," and "He causes the Śunaḥśepa story to be recited."
In this regard, just as the sacrifices are primary,
it is likewise appropriate for the gambling and other such acts to be primary as well;
since the fact of their being recited within the context is the same in both cases— this being the position reached, [the author replies:]

We reply: In the injunction "A king desiring sovereignty should sacrifice with the Rājasūya," the sacrifice denoted by the verbal root is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) expressed by the verbal suffix.
Since the word *rājasūya* has no well-known meaning [other than this], it becomes the name (*nāmadheya*) of that sacrifice through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

This being the case, because the sentence concludes with the meaning "One should bring about sovereignty by means of the Rājasūya sacrifice," the sacrifices such as the Anumati and others possess the fruit and thus constitute the primary acts (*aṅgin*).
In its proximity, an act such as gambling that is heard [in the text] but yields no fruit is an auxiliary of the sacrifice.
(Regarding the second section [Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.3–4], which concerns whether the *devana* belongs as a subsidiary part to the entire *rājasūya*: JaiS 4.4.3:
That which stands in the middle belongs to that [sacrifice] within whose midst it is situated. JaiS 4.4.4:
Or rather, it should belong to all [the sacrifices] because they are equal in being enjoined; for its mention in the middle is not stated for the purpose of indicating location.)
The second section (adhikaraṇa) formulates [the following]: Is this [rite] an auxiliary to the single Abhiṣecya sacrifice alone, or to the entire [Sattra] sacrifice?
The first [sequence] is due to the displacement of the Rājasūya; the latter is due to the context.

— Regarding that which was stated, namely that the subsidiary acts such as the gambling (devana) and so forth belong to the sacrifice, those are subsidiaries of only one [part], the consecration (abhiṣecanīya) Soma-sacrifice.
Why?
Because of displacement (*apakarṣāt*).
Although the gambling and other acts are recited in proximity to the consecration (*abhiṣecanīya*), they follow after the procedure for that consecration.

Nevertheless, they are displaced from their position in the midday libation (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*). By the statement, "The King, as the sacrificer, is consecrated in response to the *Māhendra* hymn," the king's consecration is displaced to the time of the hymn during the midday pressing.
When that [consecration] is displaced, the displacement of the gambling and other acts previously prescribed before it is established by the very nature of the situation.

Therefore, since it falls within the scope of the procedure for the Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice—just like the Māhendra-stotra and other such elements—it follows that the *devana* (gambling) and other rites are subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the Abhiṣecanīya itself.

This being the position reached, we reply: Is proximity (*saṃnidhi*) the authority for its being a subsidiary, or is it the intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*) constructed by the performance (*prayoga*)?
In either case, because the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the main context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) is more powerful, the consecration and other rites are subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the Rājasūya.
Furthermore, the word "Rājasūya" denotes all the sacrifices, including the Anumati and others.
Therefore, this [consecration] is a subsidiary of all of them.

However, since the performance [of the *rājasūya*] is required at a certain point within the *rājasūya*, it is performed at the time of the *māhendra* stotra during the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice by virtue of the force of the scriptural injunction.

(Third Section: On the fact that the *saumya* and other offerings belong to the time of the *upasad*s; Sūtras 5–6) Jai_4.4.5: And when there is no distinction of context, both [the connection with the *prāyaṇīya* and the *upasad*s] would be contradictory. Jai_4.4.6: Or rather, it should be merely a time [for the *saumya*], because no specific distinction is observed.
Starting with *Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya* 4.4.4–5,
the third section formulates the following:
Should one perform the *saumya* [offering] before the *upasad* rites?
The relationship of principal and subordinate, or the time [of performance], is understood from the sentence; of these, the former is perceived first.
"In front" (purastāt) indicates time here; therefore, it is a rule regarding time.
[The mention of] "Saumya" and so forth is not a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of anything, because it is desired by others as a primary element (*pradhāna*), like other sacrifices.
In the Rājasūya, those sacrifices denoted by the term *saṃsṛp* consist of the offering to Agni on eight potsherds (*āgneyāṣṭākapāla*) and others.
Among those [offerings], the eighth, ninth, and tenth belong to Soma, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu respectively.
With reference to them, this scriptural statement is handed down: "Before the Upasads, they proceed with the offering to Soma;
between [the Upasads], with that to Tvaṣṭṛ..."
"By means of the Vaiṣṇava [offering] at the end.

This statement enjoins the performance of the three offerings beginning with the Saumya at the commencement, middle, and conclusion of the Upasads that have been extended by analogy to this Soma sacrifice within the Rājasūya.
When it is argued that, based on this statement, the *saumya* and other offerings are subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the *upasad*s,
we reply: because the genitive case in the word "of the *upasad*s" (*upasadām*) is construed with the temporal term "before" (*purastāt*),
this sentence is intended to establish a specific temporal relationship for the *saumya* and other offerings.

But it does not have the status of being a subordinate part (aṅga) to another principal part (aṅgin). Therefore, qualities such as gentleness (*saumya*) and so forth are not the subordinate parts of anything;
rather, like consent (*anumati*) and other such acts, they are themselves primary (*pradhāna*).
[In the fourth [section], regarding the adhikaraṇa on the subsidiary nature of the Āmanahomas to the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice, the sūtra states:
"Or rather, because the stated reason applies, that which possesses a fruit would be the primary [act] for the other. (Jaimini 4.4.7)
The fourth section formulates the problem: Is the *amanahoma* primary, or is it a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice?
Because there is no contradiction, it would be primary; because it serves a specific purpose, it would be a subsidiary part.
In the section on optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi-kāṇḍa*), it is heard: "One desiring a village should offer the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
Therein, the *āmanahoma* oblations are prescribed: "He offers three oblations with the formula, 'O gods, of the mind, of the mind...
These *āmanahoma* oblations are of equal primary status (*samapradhāna*) with the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice itself.
If it is argued that there is no contradiction whatsoever in their being primary,
since we observe the primacy of many [subsidiaries] in rites such as the Āgneya and in acts such as consent (*anumati*), we say:
not so.

Just as the connection of many [subsidiaries] with the fruit is understood from the sentence "One desiring heaven [should sacrifice] by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa" and from the sentence "One desiring sovereignty [should sacrifice] by means of the Rājasūya," so it is with the Āmanahoma offerings;
for if there were no connection with a fruit, their status as primary acts would be untenable.

The sentence, "One desiring a village should perform the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice," [indicates that] the Āmana-homas, which are taught in proximity to the Sāṃgrahaṇī and are themselves fruitless, are its subsidiary parts.

(Regarding the fifth section on the obligatory nature of the *dadhi-graha*, Sūtras 8–11: The *dadhi-graha* is occasional (*naimittika*), because of its connection with a scriptural injunction [Jaimini 4.4.8]. And it is also obligatory (*nitya*), because of the word "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) [Jaimini 4.4.9].
And because of the appearance of all forms [of the sacrifice]. Jaimini 4.4.10:

Or rather, it must be eternal, for it is an explanatory praise (arthavāda); there is no connection between those two and the ritual act, and because an interruption is subject to destruction. Jaimini 4.4.11.
He formulates the fifth section:
"Whether it be considered obligatory or occasional, the *dadhi-graha* (curd-offering) is indeed obligatory;
yet, due to the intervention of other deities and its status as the foremost (*jyaiṣṭhya*), it possesses a dual nature."
For here, words such as "if" (yadi) do not indicate a causal condition (*nimitta*);
therefore, this [act] does not have the nature of a condition, and its eternality alone is appropriate.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "Whatever deity the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer should omit..."
"Those two [ears] of hers are torn away;
when he draws the *dadhigraha* belonging to Prajāpati, he indeed pacifies her. Thus, this *dadhigraha* is of a dual nature, being both obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*).
Why?
Because there exists evidence for two distinct forms:
since it is stated that, after first presenting the agitation of that deity by means of another deity, its pacification is then brought about by a *graha*.
The obstacle is the sign (nimitta), and the cup (graha) is that which possesses the sign (naimittika); thus it appears.
Likewise, its seniority is traditionally taught: "This is indeed the eldest of the cups."
Seniority (jyeṣṭhatva) means being praiseworthy;
and that is possible only if it is eternal. Since that which is occasional is contingent, it is not praiseworthy.
If it is argued that it is therefore of a dual nature due to the power of two causes,
it is not so;
for there is no causal basis for the intervention of another deity.
If [the action] were based on a cause (nimitta), the word "yadi" would be connected [to it],
or the locative case would be heard;
or else the word "yat" would be used in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer, who are the agents of the interruption.

This is because such [contingent] injunctions are observed in cases where the occasion is universally accepted, as in: "If the Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara-sāman, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu," and "One offers an oblation when [the vessel] is broken," or "He who piles the fire-altar without having carried the fire in the pan for a year," and so forth.
Therefore, it is appropriate that the Dadhi-graha (curd-cup) is purely obligatory.
The presentation of the resolution regarding the deities being both male and female is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended as praise for the acceptance of what is to be enjoined.
(Section 6: On the occasional nature of the Vaiśvānara sacrifice;

Sūtras 12–13) And the Vaiśvānara [offering] should be obligatory, because it has the same number as the obligatory ones. (Jaimini 4.4.12) Or rather, it is occasional, because its connection arises with that which has already been produced. (Jaimini 4.4.13)
START MJaiNy 4.4.9:
The sixth section formulates [the inquiry]: Is the Vaiśvānara sacrifice obligatory or occasional, given its connection with the piling of the fire-altar (citi)?
"Because of the word 'as before' (puravat), it is permanent; and because there is no contradiction, the latter [is also permanent].

In the context of the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), it is heard in scripture: "Verily, he who piles the fire-altar without having carried the fire in the *ukhya* for a year perishes, just as an embryo perishes prematurely."
"He shall suffer such pain;
he should first offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara"— here,
*ukhā* means a cooking-pot (*piṭhara*).
Having prepared that fire-pan (ukhā) with the mantras recited in the section beginning with "yañjānaḥ prathamaṃ manaḥ," and having placed the fire within that pan,
he should suspend it from a carrying-pole (śikya) with six or twelve cross-beams (udyāma).
Having tied that fire-stick (śikya) to one's own neck and maintained that principal fire for a year, one should thereafter pile the fire-altar with bricks;
for if it is not maintained, there would be destruction, like the miscarriage of an incomplete fetus.
Therefore, one should perform the Vaiśvānareṣṭi even before the piling of the fire-altar; this is the meaning.

If it is argued that, just as with the statement regarding obstacles, the statement regarding non-maintenance is merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda), and thus the Vaiśvānareṣṭi is obligatory—this is not so.

Because, by the force of the word *yaḥ* (who) which is coreferential with the agent in the statement, "The man who, having not maintained the sacred fires, piles them, should offer [this oblation]," there appears a relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*) between the non-maintenance and the sacrifice.
Furthermore, it is contradictory for the *dadhi-graha*, which is obligatory (*nitya*), to have the character of being contingent (*naimittikatva*) in the sense of being optional (*pākṣikatva*).
But here, since there is no evidence for eternality, there is no contradiction in the fact that it is exclusively occasional (naimittika).
(Regarding the seventh section [Sūtras 14–18], which concerns the occasional nature of the sixth layer in the seventh [book]:
The sixth layer is as before, because of its prior occurrence;
and because it is enumerated as equal in number with them. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.14–15)
And because the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is thus justified: Jaimini 4.4.16.
Or rather, there should be a single layer (ekaciti), for it is enjoined by a specific occasion once [the previous] has been completed; Jaimini 4.4.17.
Because of the contradiction, it should have the same number as those [layers]; Jaimini 4.4.18.
The seventh section begins with *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 4.4.10 and formulates the following inquiry:
Is the sixth layer permanent or not? It is permanent, because it is required by the five [layers] preceding the fire-altar.
The last [alternative] is based on the fact that non-establishment has been made the reason for the removal [of the fire].
Regarding this, it is heard in the *Agni* section: "The year indeed pushes him away from his foundation, he who, having piled the fire-altar, does not find a firm footing."
"There are five preceding layers; then one piles the sixth layer.
On a plot of ground measuring one fathom (vyāma) that has been ploughed with a plough, a site is constructed in the shape of a bird using various kinds of bricks.
This is the *citi*;
five such *citis* are first constructed,
and after that comes the sixth *citi*.
In that regard, if one follows the etymological derivation "the sixth is that which completes the six," then the first five [bricks] must be considered in relation to the sixth;
otherwise, it would be impossible for them to fulfill the number six.
Therefore, if it is argued that [the sixth brick] is obligatory because of the rule regarding a single performance, just like the other bricks—[we reply: no.

Not so; for when the construction of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) has been completed by the preceding five layers according to the rule "having piled the fire" (*agniṃ citvā*), the sixth layer is subsequently enjoined by means of the relative pronoun *yaḥ*—which is coreferential with the agent—as having non-establishment as its occasion, in the statement: "He who does not find firm footing here piles the sixth. Thus, the sixth layer is contingent (*naimittikī*).
Therefore— the fire is eternally five-layered, whereas it is single-layered for occasional rites; thus, there is unity of application.
However, the suffix denoting completion (*pūraṇapratyaya*) is appropriate with respect to the naming [of the layers]:
"The first five layers have been named;
now he piles the sixth layer which is yet to be named."
Such is the analysis of the statement.

(Eighth Section: On the fact that the Pitṛyajña is not an auxiliary [of the Darśapūrṇamāsa]; Sūtras 19–21) The Pitṛyajña would not be an auxiliary because it has its own specific time. (Jaimini 4.4.19) Because it is enumerated as being equal [to the other subsidiaries]. (Jaimini 4.4.20)
"And because it is seen [even] when [the original act] is prohibited" (Jaimini 4.4.21). He formulates the eighth section as follows:
"Is the Piṇḍapitṛyajña an auxiliary part of a sacrifice, or not? For it occurs within a sacrifice;

[one might argue] no, because of the statement that it is performed without beans (*amaṣāsyā*). [The author replies: Not so, because its timing is stated [independently], and thus it serves the purpose of man (*puruṣārtha*). This is recorded in the tradition: "On the new moon day, in the afternoon, they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña."
If it is argued that this Piṇḍapitṛyajña is an auxiliary part of the sacrifice (kratvaṅga) because it is enjoined in connection with the rite denoted by the word "amāvāsyā," it is not so;
for the word "amāvāsyā" denotes time.
However, this word is used figuratively in the sense of an action (*karman*).
Nor should it be argued that even if there is no status as an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) through syntactical connection (*vākya*), there is such a status through context (*prakaraṇa*);
for that [context] is taught independently (*anārabhyādhīta*).
Therefore, this is the human goal.
(Regarding the ninth section [Adhikaraṇa] on the rope being an auxiliary of the sacrificial post, Sūtras 22–24:

The rope should be an auxiliary of the animal, because it is prescribed upon the arrival of that [animal]. (Jaimini 4.4.22) Or rather, it is an auxiliary of the sacrificial post, because it is a consecratory act for it. (Jaimini 4.4.23)
"And the explanatory passage (arthavāda) has that as its purpose" (Jaimini 4.4.24).
[The author] formulates the ninth section (adhikaraṇa):
The rope is secondary; it serves the purpose of the animal or the purpose of the sacrificial post because of its connection with the animal.
It serves the purpose of the animal when [the text says] "having encircled the threefold [rope]," whereas it goes to the post when [the text says] "having encircled the post.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "Having taken the Āśvina cup, having encircled the sacrificial post with the threefold [rope], he dedicates the Agneya Savanīya animal."

In this regard, since the *savanīya* animal sacrifice is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *agnīṣomīya*, the encircling of the sacrificial post (*yūpaparivyāṇa*)—which is obtained through the force of the archetypal injunction (*codaka*)—is restated for the purpose of indicating the time; subsequently, the bringing forward of the animal (*upākaraṇa*), characterized by the threefold rope (*trivṛdraśanā*), is enjoined.

If it is argued that, therefore, because the rope is connected to the animal here, and because it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) by preventing the animal from wandering hither and thither through its act of binding, the rope is for the sake of the animal.
Not so;

because the relationship between the subordinate and the principal is established by the instrumental case "with the triple-stranded" (*trivṛtā*) and the accusative case "the sacrificial post" (*yūpam*),
and because an immediate syntactic connection is obtained, the rope is for the purpose of the sacrificial post.
The time, however, is indicated by the very statement, "Having taken the Āśvina cup.
Just as the departure of the animal is [the purpose], so too the strengthening of the sacrificial post is a visible purpose.
Nor should it be argued that the strength [of the post] is already established through the injunction itself by means of the encircling with a rope (*parivyāṇa*).

Since that [first] success has already occurred through the previous injunction itself by virtue of accepting the encircling with a second girdle as a subsidiary part, therefore—this second girdle is for the sake of the sacrificial post (yūpa). MJaiNyC_4,4.12 //
(Regarding the tenth section on the status of the *svaru* as an accessory to the animal sacrifice, Sūtras 25–28:
And the *svaru* [is an accessory] because it is a single part [of the sacrificial post]. (Jaimini 4.4.25) And its purchase is like that of its [the post’s] accessory. (Jaimini 4.4.26)
Or rather, that [offering] would have the animal limb as its object;
[the statement regarding the purchase] would be a figurative expression for the act of redemption.
The tenth section formulates the problem:

Is the *svaru* (wooden chip) an accessory (*aṅga*) to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), or is it an accessory to the animal (*paśu*) because of the statement "the *svaru* belongs to the post"? The former view [is suggested] by that statement; however, because of the statement "one should anoint the animal with the *svaru*," its status as an accessory to the animal is clear.

Regarding the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, it is heard in the scripture: "He makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)" and "He anoints the animal with the *svaru*. If it is argued that the *svaru* is an accessory (*aṅga*) to the sacrificial post because its connection to the post is stated there, it is not so.

Since the relationship between the subordinate and the principal is understood through the instrumental and accusative cases in the phrase "svaruṇā paśum," the genitive case—which expresses a general relation—can also be interpreted as intending that the *svaru* is produced by the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Therefore, the *svaru* is an accessory to the animal sacrifice.
(Eleventh [Adhikaraṇa] – Sūtras 29–38: On the status of the Āghāra-offerings and others as subsidiaries.

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, all the offerings are primary acts, because there is no distinction [between them]. (Jaimini 4.4.29) Or rather, some are subsidiaries, those in which there is praise by way of being a subsidiary; for the connection is common [to both]. (Jaimini 4.4.30)
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose [Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.31].
But the remaining reason is that the subordinate element exists within the primary elements [Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.32].
