There is no observation of another purpose when it has not been stated, because it is for the sake of another [Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.33].

The application of the two designations [of the principal and the subordinate] occurs through direct statement and through designation; furthermore, that which possesses fruit is the primary [act], and that which is not connected [to a fruit] in its proximity should be a subordinate member (*aṅga*), because it shares in the cause and because no connection with another is heard. (Jaimini 4.4.34) Moreover, qualities are enjoined in connection with names, and they are not applicable to subordinate members. (Jaimini 4.4.35)
The scriptural mention of the cause is equal [to that of other rites], and the relationship between the subsidiary and the principal exists [therein].

(Jaimini 4.4.36) Since the connection is established at the time of origination, there should therefore be an instruction regarding the subsidiaries. (Jaimini 4.4.37) And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose. (Jaimini 4.4.38)
The fourteenth section of the fourth chapter of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra formulates the following point:
Is the Āghāra-libation and so forth primary, or is it not, as in the case of the Āgneya and other sacrifices?
The six [principal sacrifices] are established by name; the remaining others are so designated through their connection with the constituent parts (aṅga).
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Āghāra, Ājyabhāgas, Prayājas, Anuyājas, and so forth, are prescribed without a specific connection to time.
The six sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya, however, are enjoined with a connection to time.
In this regard— just as the primary status of the Āgneya and other sacrifices has been accepted, so too must it be accepted for the Āghāra and other offerings;
just as in the Rājasūya sacrifice there is equal primacy among the many distinct iṣṭis, animal sacrifices, and Soma sacrifices, so it is here.

Furthermore, the recitation within a single context (*ekaprakaraṇapāṭha*) is identical in both cases. Therefore, when it is argued that the *āghāra* offerings and the *āgneya* sacrifices possess equal primary status (*samapradhānya*), we reply: In the statement, "A king desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the Rājasūya," the word "Rājasūya" applies because of its connection to a king; thus, it refers to all the rites read within that single context which have a king as their performer.
It is the name of sacrifices.

However, the words *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa*, being denotative of time, acquire the status of names for the six sacrifices—the Āgneya and the others—precisely because they are enjoined in connection with those times.

Consequently, by the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa," it is understood through the force of those names that only the six sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya are the primary [acts] connected with the fruit.

But other [rites], such as the *ājyabhāga* and *āghāra*, which lack those names and are fruitless, are the remnants of the *āgneya* and other offerings. This being the case, their praise as constituent parts (*aṅga*) is appropriate:
"These two are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice."
When it is said, "The two *ājyabhāga* offerings," the two *ājyabhāgas* are praised as being limbs (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, which is the possessor of limbs (*aṅgin*).

When it is said, "In that the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are performed, a coat of mail (*varman*) is indeed made for this sacrifice," the *prayājas* and *anuyājas* are praised as a protective armor (*varman*) that benefits the body of the sacrifice.
In this same manner, examples such as the *āghāra* libations and others should be cited.
And this is possible only when there is similarity;
therefore, the substratum and the other factors do not possess primary status.
(Regarding the section on the subsidiarity of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites within the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, Sūtras 39–41:

In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, [all parts] are equal, for the cause is undifferentiated. (Jaimini 4.4.39) But because the qualities are connected with the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), there is a scriptural statement of the cause; therefore, the *Soma* sacrifice should be the primary [element]. (Jaimini 4.4.40)
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.41).
He formulates the twelfth section as follows:
Is the *dīkṣaṇīyā* not primary, or is it primary because of its similarity to the *soma* sacrifice? "That for which the *stomas* are in the *jyotis*"—thus, the *jyotiṣṭoma* alone is primary.
In the context of the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma*," there are the *soma* sacrifices such as the *aindravāyava-graha* and others.
The *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other offerings, as well as the *agnīṣomīya* and other animal sacrifices, have been prescribed in the sacred texts.

In this regard, it might be argued that—just as the name *darśapūrṇamāsa* applies specifically to those sacrifices belonging to the side of Agni and others—the name *jyotiṣṭoma* lacks any reason to belong exclusively to the Soma-sacrifices; rather, like the name *rājasūya*, it is common to all the sacrifices under discussion.
Consequently, even the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites that are recited alongside the Soma-sacrifices would possess primary status.
This is not so.
Because there exists a reason for favoring the *somayāga* [soma-sacrifice]:
for its etymological derivation is "that sacrifice whose *stomas* are the luminaries (*jyotis*) is the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
For this very reason, the *Brāhmaṇa* states: "The *Trivṛt*..."
The fifteenth,
the seventeenth,
and the twenty-first.
"Or rather, these very stomas of this [sacrifice] are those lights.
The "light-ness" (*jyotiṣṭva*) of the *stomas* consists in their being illuminators of the sacrifice;
for neither the ritual acts nor the sacrificial animals appear as being joined with the *stomas* such as the *trivṛt* and others.

Therefore—since it is understood that only the Soma sacrifices, by virtue of the name "Jyotiṣṭoma," are connected with the fruit [of the action], the iṣṭis and animal sacrifices, being fruitless, are not primary; thus, the Soma sacrifices alone possess primacy.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter, and the fourth chapter is completed, in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* composed by the venerable Mādhava.
